13.7 Tangent Planes and Normal Lines

Larson & Edwards 7e (pp. 931–939) & Dr. Alhumaidy Notes — Gradient Normal Vectors $\nabla F(P_0)$, Tangent Planes, Normal Lines, Surface Intersection Curves, Angle of Inclination & Parallel/Perpendicular Plane Conditions.

What You Already Know

In Calculus I, a differentiable curve $y = f(x)$ has tangent line $y - y_0 = f'(x_0)(x - x_0)$ using a single slope $f'(x_0)$. In Section 11.5, you saw that any plane through $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ with normal vector $\mathbf{n} = \langle A, B, C \rangle$ satisfies $\mathbf{n} \cdot \langle x - x_0, y - y_0, z - z_0 \rangle = 0$, and any line through $P_0$ in direction $\mathbf{v}$ uses that same vector for its direction numbers. And in Section 13.6, you proved that the 2D gradient $\nabla f(x_0, y_0)$ is always orthogonal to the level curve $f(x, y) = k$. Section 13.7 lifts that exact orthogonality idea one dimension higher into 3D space.

Core Concept • §1

1. Tangent Plane & Normal Line via $\nabla F(x_0, y_0, z_0)$

Intuition: Imagine resting a rigid flat pane of glass against a smooth sphere or bowl at a single point $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$, while driving a straight pin through $P_0$ perpendicular to that glass pane (Textbook p. 931, Billiard Ball Exploration & Figures 13.55–13.56). The flat glass is the tangent plane, and the perpendicular pin (the line of impact) is the normal line. Writing a surface in general 3-variable form $F(x, y, z) = 0$ puts $x$, $y$, and $z$ on equal footing so the 3D gradient $\nabla F(P_0)$ gives that perpendicular direction in one step (Textbook pp. 931–932, Example 1 & Figure 13.57).

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Larson writes gradients with $\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}$ (Textbook p. 934), whereas Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes (pp. 932, 934) use component brackets $\nabla F(x_0, y_0, z_0) = \langle F_x, F_y, F_z \rangle \neq \langle 0, 0, 0 \rangle$ and solve explicit surfaces directly via $z = f(x_0, y_0) + f_x(x_0, y_0)(x - x_0) + f_y(x_0, y_0)(y - y_0)$ rather than $f_x(x-x_0)+f_y(y-y_0)-(z-z_0)=0$. Both forms describe the exact same plane; follow your instructor’s notation for speed on exams.
Level surface $F(x,y,z)=0$ Tangent plane through $P_0$ Normal vector $\nabla F(P_0)$ & normal line Tangent vectors $\mathbf{r}'(t_0)$ in the plane

Notice that $\nabla F(P_0)$ makes a $90^\circ$ angle with every tangent vector $\mathbf{r}'(t_0)$ lying in the tangent plane at $P_0$ (cf. Textbook p. 932, Figure 13.57).

Formulas (Textbook p. 932, Theorem 13.13 & p. 933): Let $F$ be differentiable at $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on $F(x, y, z) = 0$ with $\nabla F(P_0) = \langle F_x(P_0), F_y(P_0), F_z(P_0) \rangle \neq \langle 0, 0, 0 \rangle$.

  • Tangent plane to $F(x, y, z) = 0$: $$F_x(P_0)(x - x_0) + F_y(P_0)(y - y_0) + F_z(P_0)(z - z_0) = 0$$
  • Special explicit case $z = f(x, y)$: Setting $F(x, y, z) = f(x, y) - z = 0$ yields $\nabla F(P_0) = \langle f_x(x_0, y_0), f_y(x_0, y_0), -1 \rangle$, so: $$z = f(x_0, y_0) + f_x(x_0, y_0)(x - x_0) + f_y(x_0, y_0)(y - y_0)$$
  • Normal line at $P_0$: $$\frac{x - x_0}{F_x(P_0)} = \frac{y - y_0}{F_y(P_0)} = \frac{z - z_0}{F_z(P_0)} \quad \text{(provided } F_x, F_y, F_z \neq 0 \text{)}$$

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 937, Ex. 18): Find the tangent plane and symmetric normal line to the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9$ at $P_0(1, 2, 2)$.

Set $F(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 9 = 0$. Then $\nabla F = \langle 2x, 2y, 2z \rangle$, so $\nabla F(1, 2, 2) = \langle 2, 4, 4 \rangle$ (parallel to $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1, 2, 2 \rangle$). Thus the tangent plane is $1(x - 1) + 2(y - 2) + 2(z - 2) = 0 \implies x + 2y + 2z = 9$, and the symmetric normal line is $\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y - 2}{2} = \dfrac{z - 2}{2}$.

Why It Works (Chain Rule Proof, Textbook p. 932 & p. 936 Theorem 13.14): For any differentiable curve $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle x(t), y(t), z(t) \rangle$ on $S$ passing through $P_0 = \mathbf{r}(t_0)$, we have $F(x(t), y(t), z(t)) = 0$ for all $t$. Differentiating by the Chain Rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}[F(\mathbf{r}(t))] = \nabla F(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) = 0$. Evaluating at $t = t_0$ shows $\nabla F(P_0) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t_0) = 0$, so $\nabla F(P_0)$ is orthogonal to every tangent vector at $P_0$. Unlike the 2D gradient $\nabla f(x, y)$ (which lives in the $xy$-plane and is normal to level curves), $\nabla F(x, y, z)$ lives in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and is normal to level surfaces (Textbook p. 936).

Quick Check 1: Which vector is normal to the surface $z = x^2 - 3y$ at the point $P_0(2, 1, 1)$?
(A) $\langle 4, -3, 1 \rangle$ (B) $\langle 4, -3, -1 \rangle$ (C) $\langle 4, -3, 0 \rangle$ (D) $\langle 2, -3, -1 \rangle$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) $\langle 4, -3, -1 \rangle$. Move $z$ to the same side: $F(x, y, z) = x^2 - 3y - z = 0$. Then $\nabla F(x, y, z) = \langle 2x, -3, -1 \rangle$, so $\nabla F(2, 1, 1) = \langle 4, -3, -1 \rangle$.
Core Concept • §2

2. Tangent Line to the Intersection Curve of Two Surfaces

Intuition: When two smooth surfaces $F(x, y, z) = 0$ and $G(x, y, z) = 0$ slice through each other, their seam forms a 3D space curve $C$. At any shared point $P_0$ on $C$, the tangent line to $C$ is simply the line where the two tangent planes intersect — meaning its direction vector $\mathbf{v}$ must stay perpendicular to both $\nabla F(P_0)$ and $\nabla G(P_0)$ at the same time (Textbook p. 935, Figure 13.61; Alhumaidy notes p. 937).

$\nabla F(P_0)$ normal to $F=0$ $\nabla G(P_0)$ normal to $G=0$ Cross product $\mathbf{v} = \nabla F(P_0) \times \nabla G(P_0)$

Because the intersection curve lies on both surfaces simultaneously, its tangent direction $\mathbf{v}$ is orthogonal to both $\nabla F(P_0)$ and $\nabla G(P_0)$, matching their cross product.

Formula (Textbook p. 935): If $\nabla F(P_0) \times \nabla G(P_0) = \langle a, b, c \rangle \neq \langle 0, 0, 0 \rangle$, then parametric equations of the tangent line to the intersection curve at $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ are:

$$x = x_0 + at, \qquad y = y_0 + bt, \qquad z = z_0 + ct$$

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 935, Example 5): Find parametric equations for the tangent line to the intersection of the ellipsoid $x^2 + 2y^2 + 2z^2 = 20$ and the paraboloid $x^2 + y^2 + z = 4$ at $(0, 1, 3)$.

Set $F = x^2 + 2y^2 + 2z^2 - 20$ and $G = x^2 + y^2 + z - 4$. At $(0, 1, 3)$: $\nabla F(0, 1, 3) = \langle 0, 4, 12 \rangle$ and $\nabla G(0, 1, 3) = \langle 0, 2, 1 \rangle$. Thus: $$\mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 0 & 4 & 12 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \langle 4(1) - 12(2),\; 0,\; 0 \rangle = \langle -20, 0, 0 \rangle$$ Dividing by $-20$ gives direction numbers $1, 0, 0$, so the tangent line is $x = t,\; y = 1,\; z = 3$.

Why It Works: Any curve $C$ shared by $F = 0$ and $G = 0$ has tangent vector $\mathbf{v}$ at $P_0$ inside both tangent planes, forcing $\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla F(P_0) = 0$ and $\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla G(P_0) = 0$. The cross product $\nabla F(P_0) \times \nabla G(P_0)$ produces a vector perpendicular to both normals.

Quick Check 2 (Textbook p. 937, Ex. 27): Which vector is parallel to the tangent line to the intersection curve of $x^2 + y^2 = 2$ and $z = x$ at $(1, 1, 1)$?
(A) $\langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle$ (B) $\langle 1, -1, 1 \rangle$ (C) $\langle 1, -1, 0 \rangle$ (D) $\langle 2, 2, -1 \rangle$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) $\langle 1, -1, 1 \rangle$. Using $F = x^2 + y^2 - 2$ and $G = x - z$: $\nabla F(1, 1, 1) = \langle 2, 2, 0 \rangle$ and $\nabla G(1, 1, 1) = \langle 1, 0, -1 \rangle$. Their cross product is $\langle -2, 2, -2 \rangle = -2\langle 1, -1, 1 \rangle$.
Core Concept • §3

3. Angle of Inclination of a Tangent Plane

Intuition: The angle of inclination $\theta$ ($0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$) of a tangent plane is the acute tilt angle between the tangent plane and the flat horizontal $xy$-plane (Textbook p. 935, Figure 13.62). Imagine resting a flat board on the floor and tilting it up by $\theta$: a perpendicular pole glued straight out of the board tilts away from the vertical vector $\mathbf{k} = \langle 0, 0, 1 \rangle$ by that exact same angle $\theta$.

Tangent plane tilted by $\theta$ Vertical normal $\mathbf{k} = \langle 0,0,1\rangle$ Surface normal $\mathbf{n} = \nabla F(P_0)$ Equal acute angles $\theta \approx 35.3^\circ$

Side cross-section drawn to exact scale for Textbook p. 936 Example 6 ($\theta = \arccos\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \approx 35.3^\circ$): tilting the plane by $\theta$ tilts its normal $\mathbf{n}$ away from $\mathbf{k}$ by the same angle $\theta$.

Formulas (Textbook pp. 935–936): Since $\mathbf{k} = \langle 0, 0, 1 \rangle$ has length $\|\mathbf{k}\| = 1$, the acute angle $\theta \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ between a plane with normal $\mathbf{n} = \nabla F(P_0)$ and the $xy$-plane satisfies:

$$\cos\theta = \frac{|\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{k}|}{\|\mathbf{n}\|\,\|\mathbf{k}\|} = \frac{|F_z(P_0)|}{\sqrt{F_x(P_0)^2 + F_y(P_0)^2 + F_z(P_0)^2}} \qquad \text{or for } z = f(x, y): \quad \cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{[f_x(x_0, y_0)]^2 + [f_y(x_0, y_0)]^2 + 1}}$$

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 936, Example 6): Find the angle of inclination of the tangent plane to the ellipsoid $\dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac{y^2}{12} + \dfrac{z^2}{3} = 1$ at $(2, 2, 1)$.

Let $F(x, y, z) = \dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac{y^2}{12} + \dfrac{z^2}{3} - 1$. Then $\nabla F(x, y, z) = \left\langle \dfrac{x}{6},\; \dfrac{y}{6},\; \dfrac{2z}{3} \right\rangle$, so $\nabla F(2, 2, 1) = \left\langle \dfrac{1}{3},\; \dfrac{1}{3},\; \dfrac{2}{3} \right\rangle$. Therefore: $$\cos\theta = \frac{2/3}{\sqrt{(1/3)^2 + (1/3)^2 + (2/3)^2}} = \frac{2/3}{\sqrt{6}/3} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \implies \theta = \arccos\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \approx 35.3^\circ$$

Why It Works: By Section 11.5, the acute dihedral angle between two planes equals the acute angle between their normal vectors. Absolute value $|\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{k}|$ guarantees $\cos\theta \ge 0$ so $\theta \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ regardless of whether $\nabla F$ points upward or downward (e.g. $F = f(x, y) - z$ vs. $F = z - f(x, y)$).

Quick Check 3 (Textbook p. 937, Ex. 35): What is the angle of inclination $\theta$ of the tangent plane to $x^2 - y^2 + z = 0$ at $(1, 2, 3)$?
(A) $\arccos\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{21}}\right)$ (B) $\arcsin\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{21}}\right)$ (C) $\arccos\!\left(\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{21}}\right)$ (D) $0$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (A) $\arccos\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{21}}\right)$. Here $F(x,y,z)=x^2-y^2+z$, so $\nabla F(1,2,3)=\langle 2, -4, 1\rangle$ and $\|\nabla F\|=\sqrt{4+16+1}=\sqrt{21}$. Thus $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|1|}{\sqrt{21}}$.
Core Concept • §4

4. Locating Horizontal, Parallel, or Perpendicular Tangent Planes

Intuition: Instead of being handed $P_0$ directly, KFUPM exam problems frequently ask you to find the point $(a, b, c)$ on a surface where its tangent plane satisfies a geometric condition — such as being horizontal, parallel to a given plane, or perpendicular to a given line or second surface (Textbook pp. 937–938, Exercises 37–51; Alhumaidy notes pp. 937–938). Every one of these problems translates into a simple vector equation on $\nabla F(x, y, z)$.

Surface gradient $\nabla F(P_0)$ Target plane normal $\mathbf{n}$ Second surface gradient $\nabla G(P_0)$

Every geometric condition on tangent planes turns into an algebraic condition on $\nabla F(P_0)$ plus substituting back into the surface equation.

Rules & Steps (Alhumaidy notes pp. 937–938):

  • Horizontal tangent plane on $z = f(x, y)$: Set $f_x(x, y) = 0$ and $f_y(x, y) = 0$, solve for $(x_0, y_0)$, then substitute back into $z = f(x_0, y_0)$ to get $z_0$ (Alhumaidy p. 937).
  • Tangent plane parallel to a given plane $Ax + By + Cz = D$ (or perpendicular to a line with direction $\mathbf{v}$): Solve $\nabla F(x_0, y_0, z_0) = \alpha\,\mathbf{n}$ for $x_0, y_0, z_0$ in terms of the scalar $\alpha \neq 0$, then substitute into the surface equation to solve for $\alpha$ (Alhumaidy p. 938, Ex. 49).
  • Tangent surfaces / Perpendicular surfaces at $P_0$: First verify $P_0$ satisfies both surface equations; then two surfaces are tangent if $\nabla F(P_0) \parallel \nabla G(P_0)$ (same tangent plane), and perpendicular if $\nabla F(P_0) \cdot \nabla G(P_0) = 0$ (Textbook p. 938, Ex. 43–46).

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 937, Ex. 37 / Alhumaidy notes): Find the point on $z = 3 - x^2 - y^2 + 6y$ where the tangent plane is horizontal.

Set $f_x = -2x = 0 \implies x = 0$ and $f_y = -2y + 6 = 0 \implies y = 3$. Substituting $(0, 3)$ back into $z$ gives $z = 3 - 0^2 - 3^2 + 6(3) = 12$, so the point is $(0, 3, 12)$.

Quick Check 4 (KFUPM Final 251 Q9): If $(a, b, c)$ with $a < 0$ is the point on $4x^2 + 2y^2 - z^2 = 100$ where the tangent plane is parallel to the $yz$-plane ($x = 0$), what is $a^2 + b^2 + c^2$?
(A) $16$ (B) $25$ (C) $100$ (D) $225$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) $25$. The $yz$-plane has normal $\langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle$. Since $\nabla F(a, b, c) = \langle 8a, 4b, -2c \rangle = \alpha\langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle$, we get $b = 0$ and $c = 0$. Substituting into the surface gives $4a^2 = 100 \implies a = -5$ (as $a < 0$), so $(-5)^2 + 0 + 0 = 25$.
Master Formulas

Section 13.7 Formula Reference & Edge Cases

Core Equations & Required Conditions ($F$ differentiable at $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$, $\nabla F(P_0) \neq \langle 0, 0, 0 \rangle$)

  • Level Surface $F(x, y, z) = 0$ — Tangent Plane: $$F_x(P_0)(x - x_0) + F_y(P_0)(y - y_0) + F_z(P_0)(z - z_0) = 0$$
  • Explicit Surface $z = f(x, y)$ — Tangent Plane: $$z = f(x_0, y_0) + f_x(x_0, y_0)(x - x_0) + f_y(x_0, y_0)(y - y_0)$$
  • Normal Line at $P_0$: $$\begin{aligned} x &= x_0 + F_x(P_0)t, \\ y &= y_0 + F_y(P_0)t, \\ z &= z_0 + F_z(P_0)t \end{aligned} \qquad \text{or} \qquad \frac{x - x_0}{F_x(P_0)} = \frac{y - y_0}{F_y(P_0)} = \frac{z - z_0}{F_z(P_0)}$$ Edge case: If any component vanishes (say $F_x(P_0) = 0$), write $x = x_0$ separately and keep symmetric form only for nonzero denominators, e.g., $x = x_0,\; \frac{y - y_0}{F_y(P_0)} = \frac{z - z_0}{F_z(P_0)}$.
  • Tangent Line to Intersection of $F = 0$ and $G = 0$: Direction $\mathbf{v} = \nabla F(P_0) \times \nabla G(P_0)$ (requires $\mathbf{v} \neq \langle 0, 0, 0 \rangle$; otherwise the surfaces are tangent or fail regularity at $P_0$).
  • Angle of Inclination ($0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$): $$\cos\theta = \frac{|F_z(P_0)|}{\|\nabla F(P_0)\|} \qquad \text{or for } z = f(x, y): \quad \cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{[f_x(x_0, y_0)]^2 + [f_y(x_0, y_0)]^2 + 1}}$$ Edge cases: Horizontal plane $\implies \theta = 0$; vertical plane ($F_z(P_0) = 0$) $\implies \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$.
  • Quadric Tangent Shortcuts (Textbook pp. 938–939, Ex. 57–59): At $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$, tangent planes to $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} \pm \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$ take the form $\frac{x_0 x}{a^2} + \frac{y_0 y}{b^2} \pm \frac{z_0 z}{c^2} = 1$, and any tangent plane to a cone $z^2 = a^2 x^2 + b^2 y^2$ (away from $(0,0,0)$) passes through the origin $(0,0,0)$.
Exam Traps

5 Classic Mistakes (WRONG vs. RIGHT)

Trap 1 — Wrong sign on $z$ when converting $z = f(x, y)$ to $F(x, y, z) = 0$:

WrongWriting $\nabla F = \langle f_x, f_y, +1 \rangle$ for $z = x^2 + y^2$.
RightMove everything to one side: $F = f(x, y) - z = 0 \implies \nabla F = \langle f_x, f_y, -1 \rangle$.

Trap 2 — Leaving variables $(x, y, z)$ inside the normal coefficients:

Wrong$2x(x - 1) + 4y(y - 2) + 6z(z - 1) = 0$ (this is quadratic, not a plane!).
RightEvaluate $F_x, F_y, F_z$ at $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ first to get numbers before writing the plane.

Trap 3 — Ignoring the fixed coefficient or constant in KFUPM MCQs:

WrongGetting $4x - 4y + 2z + 2 = 0$ and reading $a = 4, b = -4, c = 2$ when the prompt asks for $ax + by + cz + 1 = 0$.
RightDivide the entire equation by $2$ first to match $+1$: $2x - 2y + z + 1 = 0 \implies (a,b,c) = (2,-2,1)$.

Trap 4 — Forgetting scalar $\alpha$ in parallel-plane problems or dividing by zero in symmetric equations:

WrongSetting $\nabla F(a, b, c) = \mathbf{n}$ without a scalar $\alpha$, or writing $\dfrac{z - 3}{0}$ in symmetric equations.
RightAlways solve $\nabla F(a, b, c) = \alpha\,\mathbf{n}$, and write zero-component lines as $z = 3,\; \dfrac{x-x_0}{a} = \dfrac{y-y_0}{b}$.

Trap 5 — Using $\sin\theta$ or forgetting absolute value in angle of inclination:

WrongComputing $\sin\theta = \dfrac{F_z}{\|\nabla F\|}$ or leaving a negative $\cos\theta$ from $F_z = -1$.
RightAngle between two planes uses $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|F_z(P_0)|}{\|\nabla F(P_0)\|} \ge 0$ so $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$.
Worked Examples

From Textbook Basics to KFUPM Final Level

Example 1 • Level Surface • Textbook p. 933 Example 2 & Alhumaidy Notes

Tangent Plane & Normal Line to a Hyperboloid

Find an equation of the tangent plane and symmetric equations of the normal line to the hyperboloid $z^2 - 2x^2 - 2y^2 = 12$ at $P_0(1, -1, 4)$.
Final Answer: Tangent plane: $x - y - 2z + 6 = 0$. Normal line: $\dfrac{x - 1}{-1} = \dfrac{y + 1}{1} = \dfrac{z - 4}{2}$.
1
Define $F(x, y, z) = 0$ and Compute $\nabla F$
$$F(x, y, z) = z^2 - 2x^2 - 2y^2 - 12 = 0$$ $$F_x = -4x, \qquad F_y = -4y, \qquad F_z = 2z$$
2
Evaluate $\nabla F$ at $P_0(1, -1, 4)$
$$\nabla F(1, -1, 4) = \langle -4(1),\; -4(-1),\; 2(4) \rangle = \langle -4,\; 4,\; 8 \rangle = 4\langle -1, 1, 2 \rangle$$
3
Write Tangent Plane & Normal Line Equations
$$\begin{aligned} -4(x - 1) + 4(y + 1) + 8(z - 4) &= 0 \\ -4x + 4 + 4y + 4 + 8z - 32 &= 0 \\ -4x + 4y + 8z - 24 &= 0 \\ x - y - 2z + 6 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Symmetric normal line using direction $\langle -1, 1, 2 \rangle$:

$$\frac{x - 1}{-1} = \frac{y + 1}{1} = \frac{z - 4}{2}$$
Verification: Both equations contain $P_0(1, -1, 4)$: surface gives $4^2 - 2(1)^2 - 2(-1)^2 = 16 - 2 - 2 = 12$; plane gives $1 - (-1) - 2(4) + 6 = 0$.
Example 2 • Explicit Surface & Coefficient Matching • KFUPM Final Term 253 Q11

Matching Standard Form $ax + by + cz + 1 = 0$

If $ax + by + cz + 1 = 0$ is an equation for the tangent plane to the surface $z = (x - y)^2$ at the point $(1, 2, 1)$, find $a + b + c$.
Final Answer: $a + b + c = 1$ (from $2x - 2y + z + 1 = 0$).
1
Compute Partial Derivatives at $(1, 2)$
$$f(x, y) = (x - y)^2 \implies f_x = 2(x - y), \qquad f_y = -2(x - y)$$ $$f_x(1, 2) = 2(1 - 2) = -2, \qquad f_y(1, 2) = -2(1 - 2) = 2$$
2
Assemble Explicit Tangent Plane and Match $+1$ Constant
$$\begin{aligned} z &= f(1, 2) + f_x(1, 2)(x - 1) + f_y(1, 2)(y - 2) \\ z &= 1 - 2(x - 1) + 2(y - 2) \\ z &= 1 - 2x + 2 + 2y - 4 = -2x + 2y - 1 \\ 2x - 2y + z + 1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Comparing with $ax + by + cz + 1 = 0$ gives $a = 2,\; b = -2,\; c = 1$, so $a + b + c = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1$.

Verification: Point $(1, 2, 1)$ satisfies $2(1) - 2(2) + 1 + 1 = 0$, and normal $\langle 2, -2, 1 \rangle$ equals $-\langle -2, 2, -1 \rangle = -\nabla(f - z)|_{(1,2,1)}$.
Example 3 • Surface Intersection Curve • Textbook p. 937 Ex. 31 & Alhumaidy Notes

Tangent Line Where a Sphere Meets a Plane

Find parametric equations for the tangent line to the curve of intersection of the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 14$ and the plane $x - y - z = 0$ at $P_0(3, 1, 2)$.
Final Answer: $x = 3 + t, \quad y = 1 + 5t, \quad z = 2 - 4t \quad (-\infty < t < \infty)$.
1
Find Both Gradients at $P_0(3, 1, 2)$
$$F(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 14 \implies \nabla F(3, 1, 2) = \langle 6, 2, 4 \rangle$$ $$G(x, y, z) = x - y - z \implies \nabla G(3, 1, 2) = \langle 1, -1, -1 \rangle$$
2
Compute Cross Product $\nabla F(P_0) \times \nabla G(P_0)$
$$\begin{aligned} \nabla F \times \nabla G &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 6 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} \\ &= \big(2(-1) - 4(-1)\big)\mathbf{i} - \big(6(-1) - 4(1)\big)\mathbf{j} + \big(6(-1) - 2(1)\big)\mathbf{k} \\ &= \langle 2,\; 10,\; -8 \rangle = 2\langle 1,\; 5,\; -4 \rangle \end{aligned}$$

Using simplified direction $\langle 1, 5, -4 \rangle$ through $(3, 1, 2)$ gives $x = 3 + t,\; y = 1 + 5t,\; z = 2 - 4t$.

Verification: Both dot products vanish: $\langle 1, 5, -4 \rangle \cdot \langle 6, 2, 4 \rangle = 6 + 10 - 16 = 0$, and $\langle 1, 5, -4 \rangle \cdot \langle 1, -1, -1 \rangle = 1 - 5 + 4 = 0$.
Example 4 • Horizontal Tangent Plane • Textbook p. 937 Ex. 40, Alhumaidy Notes & Final 241 Q5

Coupled System for a Horizontal Tangent Plane

Find the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface $z = 4x^2 + 4xy - 2y^2 + 8x - 5y - 4$ at which the tangent plane is horizontal.
Final Answer: $P_0\!\left(-\dfrac{1}{4},\; -\dfrac{3}{2},\; -\dfrac{5}{4}\right)$ (Exam Final 241 Q5 asks for $x_0 = -\dfrac{1}{4}$).
1
Set $z_x = 0$ and $z_y = 0$ Simultaneously
$$\begin{cases} z_x = 8x + 4y + 8 = 0 & (1) \\ z_y = 4x - 4y - 5 = 0 & (2) \end{cases}$$
2
Solve Linear System and Substitute Back for $z_0$

Add equations $(1)$ and $(2)$ directly to eliminate $y$:

$$(8x + 4y + 8) + (4x - 4y - 5) = 0 \implies 12x + 3 = 0 \implies x_0 = -\frac{1}{4}$$

Substitute $x_0 = -\frac{1}{4}$ into $(1)$: $8\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right) + 4y + 8 = 0 \implies 4y + 6 = 0 \implies y_0 = -\frac{3}{2}$.

Evaluate $z_0$ at $\left(-\frac{1}{4}, -\frac{3}{2}\right)$:

$$\begin{aligned} z_0 &= 4\left(\frac{1}{16}\right) + 4\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) - 2\left(\frac{9}{4}\right) + 8\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right) - 5\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) - 4 \\ &= \frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{2} - \frac{9}{2} - 2 + \frac{15}{2} - 4 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{9}{2} - 6 = -\frac{5}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Verification: $z_x\!\left(-\frac{1}{4}, -\frac{3}{2}\right) = -2 - 6 + 8 = 0$ and $z_y\!\left(-\frac{1}{4}, -\frac{3}{2}\right) = -1 + 6 - 5 = 0$.
Example 5 • Parallel Tangent Plane on Hyperboloid • KFUPM Final Term 242 Q9

Finding $(a, b, c)$ with $a < 0$ Using $\nabla F = \alpha\,\mathbf{n}$

If $(a, b, c)$ with $a < 0$ is the point on the hyperboloid $x^2 + 4y^2 - z^2 = -4$ where the tangent plane is parallel to the plane $2x - 4y + 3z = 1$, find $a + b + c$.
Final Answer: $(a, b, c) = (-4, 2, 6)$, so $a + b + c = -4 + 2 + 6 = 4$.
1
Equate $\nabla F(a, b, c) = \alpha\,\mathbf{n}$

With $F(x, y, z) = x^2 + 4y^2 - z^2 + 4$, we have $\nabla F(a, b, c) = \langle 2a, 8b, -2c \rangle$. The target plane has normal $\mathbf{n} = \langle 2, -4, 3 \rangle$, so for some scalar $\alpha \neq 0$:

$$\begin{cases} 2a = 2\alpha & \implies a = \alpha \\ 8b = -4\alpha & \implies b = -\dfrac{\alpha}{2} \\ -2c = 3\alpha & \implies c = -\dfrac{3\alpha}{2} \end{cases}$$
2
Substitute into the Surface and Enforce $a < 0$
$$\begin{aligned} \alpha^2 + 4\left(-\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)^2 - \left(-\frac{3\alpha}{2}\right)^2 &= -4 \\ \alpha^2 + \alpha^2 - \frac{9}{4}\alpha^2 &= -4 \\ -\frac{1}{4}\alpha^2 &= -4 \implies \alpha^2 = 16 \implies \alpha = \pm 4 \end{aligned}$$

Because $a = \alpha$ and $a < 0$, choose $\alpha = -4$: $a = -4$, $b = 2$, $c = 6$, giving $a + b + c = 4$.

$y=2$ cross-section $z^2 - x^2 = 20$ Exact tangent $2x + 3z = 10$ at $x=-4, z=6$ Gradient normal $\langle -8, 16, -12 \rangle \parallel \langle 2, -4, 3 \rangle$

Cross-section at $y = 2$ of Example 5: $x = -4$ ($a < 0$) lies on the upper branch $z = \sqrt{x^2 + 20} = 6$ with exact slope $-\frac{2}{3}$ matching $2x - 4y + 3z = 1$.

Verification: $(-4)^2 + 4(2)^2 - 6^2 = 16 + 16 - 36 = -4$, and $\nabla F(-4, 2, 6) = \langle -8, 16, -12 \rangle = -4\langle 2, -4, 3 \rangle$.
One-Screen Summary

The 5 Things to Know for the Exam

  1. Move all terms to one side ($F(x, y, z) = 0$) before taking $\nabla F$: The normal to $z = f(x, y)$ at $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is $\langle f_x, f_y, -1 \rangle$ — never $+1$ — and you must plug in $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ so your plane equation has numerical coefficients.
  2. Match the exact constant or coefficient requested: If a KFUPM question gives $ax + by + cz + 1 = 0$, rescale your entire tangent plane equation until the constant term matches $+1$ before summing $a, b, c$.
  3. Surface intersection tangent line = cross product of both gradients: Write both surfaces as $F=0$ and $G=0$, evaluate at $P_0$, and take $\mathbf{v} = \nabla F(P_0) \times \nabla G(P_0)$ (scaling out common factors is always legal).
  4. Angle of inclination $\theta \in [0, \frac{\pi}{2}]$ uses $\cos\theta$ and $|F_z|$: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|F_z(P_0)|}{\|\nabla F(P_0)\|}$; check $F_z = 0$ (vertical wall, $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$) and $F_x=F_y=0$ (horizontal plane, $\theta = 0$).
  5. Finding an unknown point $(a, b, c)$ for horizontal/parallel/perpendicular planes: Use $\nabla F(a, b, c) = \alpha\,\mathbf{n}$ (don’t forget $\alpha$!), plug into the surface equation to solve $\alpha$, and apply any sign constraint ($a < 0$ or $a > 0$).

13.8 Extrema of Functions of Two Variables

What You Already Know

In Calculus I, a function $y = f(x)$ can have a relative extremum only at a critical number where $f'(c) = 0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist, and the Second Derivative Test uses the sign of $f''(c)$ to tell peaks from valleys. On a closed interval $[a, b]$, the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees an absolute maximum and minimum found by comparing critical values with endpoints. In Section 13.7, you saw that a smooth surface $z = f(x, y)$ has a horizontal tangent plane precisely when $f_x(x_0, y_0) = 0$ and $f_y(x_0, y_0) = 0$. Section 13.8 turns those ideas into a complete toolkit for optimizing surfaces in 3D.

Core Concept • §1

1. Relative Extrema & Critical Points ($f_x = f_y = 0$ or DNE)

Intuition: Think of standing on a hilly terrain $z = f(x, y)$. A relative maximum is a hilltop higher than every point in a small circular disk around your feet, while a relative minimum is the bottom of a bowl lower than all nearby points (Textbook p. 940, Figure 13.65). At any hilltop or bowl bottom, either the ground flattens completely (a horizontal tangent plane, $f_x = 0$ and $f_y = 0$) or the surface comes to a sharp tip or ridge where at least one slope fails to exist (Textbook pp. 941–942, Figures 13.66–13.68).

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes (Textbook p. 942) write $= 0$ or $\text{DNE}$ right next to the partial derivatives so you never forget undefined points, and highlight a sharp warning (?!!) on Example 2: having only one partial equal to zero (like $f_x = 0$ along the $y$-axis) does not create a critical point unless the other partial is also zero or one of them does not exist. Always distinguish the critical point $(x_0, y_0)$ from the extreme value $f(x_0, y_0)$.
Smooth slice $y=3$ of Textbook Ex. 1 Cusp slice $y=0$ of Textbook Ex. 2 Horizontal tangent vs. vertical cusp Critical point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$

Cross-sections of Textbook pp. 942 Examples 1 and 2: relative extrema occur only at critical points, which include both flat spots ($\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$) and sharp cusps where partial derivatives fail to exist.

Definitions & Theorem (Textbook pp. 940–941):

  • Relative Extrema: For $f$ defined on a region $R$ containing $(x_0, y_0)$, $f$ has a relative minimum at $(x_0, y_0)$ if $f(x, y) \ge f(x_0, y_0)$ on some open disk containing $(x_0, y_0)$, and a relative maximum if $f(x, y) \le f(x_0, y_0)$ on some open disk containing $(x_0, y_0)$.
  • Critical Point: Let $f$ be defined on an open region $R$ containing $(x_0, y_0)$. Then $(x_0, y_0)$ is a critical point of $f$ if either: $$\text{(1) } f_x(x_0, y_0) = 0 \text{ and } f_y(x_0, y_0) = 0, \qquad \text{OR} \qquad \text{(2) } f_x(x_0, y_0) \text{ or } f_y(x_0, y_0) \text{ does not exist.}$$
  • Theorem 13.16 (Relative Extrema Occur Only at Critical Points): If $f$ has a relative extremum at $(x_0, y_0)$ on an open region $R$, then $(x_0, y_0)$ is a critical point of $f$.

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 942, Example 2 & Alhumaidy Notes): Find the relative extrema of $f(x, y) = 1 - (x^2 + y^2)^{1/3}$.

Differentiating gives: $$f_x(x, y) = -\frac{2x}{3(x^2 + y^2)^{2/3}}, \qquad f_y(x, y) = -\frac{2y}{3(x^2 + y^2)^{2/3}}$$ Both partials exist everywhere except $(0, 0)$, where the denominator is $0$ (DNE). Note that on the $y$-axis ($x = 0, y \neq 0$), $f_x = 0$ but $f_y \neq 0$, so those are not critical points. Thus $(0, 0)$ is the only critical point. Since $(x^2 + y^2)^{1/3} > 0$ for all $(x, y) \neq (0, 0)$, we have $f(x, y) < 1 = f(0, 0)$, proving $f$ has a relative maximum at $(0, 0)$ with value $1$.

Quick Check 1 (KFUPM Final 241 Q9 / Textbook p. 946 Ex. 20): The function $f(x, y) = \sqrt[3]{x^2 + y^2} + 2$ has:
(A) a saddle point at $(0, 0)$ (B) no critical points and no extrema (C) a relative maximum at $(0, 0)$ (D) a relative minimum at $(0, 0)$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (D) a relative minimum at $(0, 0)$. Both $f_x = \dfrac{2x}{3(x^2+y^2)^{2/3}}$ and $f_y = \dfrac{2y}{3(x^2+y^2)^{2/3}}$ fail to exist at $(0, 0)$, making $(0, 0)$ a critical point. Since $\sqrt[3]{x^2+y^2} \ge 0$ everywhere, $f(x, y) \ge 2 = f(0, 0)$ for all $(x, y)$.
Core Concept • §2

2. Saddle Points & The Second Partials Test

Intuition: Finding $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$ only hands you suspects — not every flat point is a peak or valley. On the hyperbolic paraboloid $f(x, y) = y^2 - x^2$ (Textbook p. 943, Figure 13.69), moving along the $y$-axis goes uphill ($f_{yy} = 2 > 0$), while moving along the $x$-axis goes downhill ($f_{xx} = -2 < 0$), creating a saddle point at $(0, 0, 0)$. Even more subtly, if $f_{xx}$ and $f_{yy}$ have the same sign, a strong mixed cross-twist $f_{xy}$ can still bend a diagonal slice the opposite way! The discriminant $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - [f_{xy}]^2$ compares pure curvature ($f_{xx}f_{yy}$) against squared diagonal twist ($[f_{xy}]^2$).

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Larson writes lowercase $d = f_{xx}(a,b)f_{yy}(a,b) - [f_{xy}(a,b)]^2$ (Textbook p. 943, Theorem 13.17), whereas Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes (pp. 942–944, 947) consistently write uppercase $D$ and organize every problem in a 4-column table: Critical Point | $f_{xx}$ | $f_{yy}$ | $f_{xy}$ | $D$. Dr. Alhumaidy also classifies quadratic polynomials like Example 1 ($2x^2+y^2+8x-6y+20$) directly with this $D$-table rather than completing the square.
Increasing / $+$ level contours Decreasing outward contours Negative saddle branches ($-$) Critical point $(a, b)$

Contour behavior around a smooth critical point $(a, b)$: $D > 0$ forces closed elliptical contours (bowl or dome), whereas $D < 0$ forces hyperbolic cross-contours of opposite signs ($y^2 - x^2 = \pm 1$).

Theorem 13.17 — Second Partials Test (Textbook p. 943): Let $f$ have continuous second partial derivatives on an open region containing $(a, b)$ with $f_x(a, b) = 0$ and $f_y(a, b) = 0$. Define the determinant discriminant:

$$D = f_{xx}(a, b)\,f_{yy}(a, b) - \big[f_{xy}(a, b)\big]^2 = \begin{vmatrix} f_{xx}(a, b) & f_{xy}(a, b) \\ f_{yx}(a, b) & f_{yy}(a, b) \end{vmatrix}$$
  • Case 1: If $D > 0$ and $f_{xx}(a, b) > 0$, then $f$ has a relative minimum at $(a, b)$.
  • Case 2: If $D > 0$ and $f_{xx}(a, b) < 0$, then $f$ has a relative maximum at $(a, b)$.
  • Case 3: If $D < 0$, then $\big(a, b, f(a, b)\big)$ is a saddle point.
  • Case 4: If $D = 0$, the test is inconclusive.

Remark (Textbook p. 943): Whenever $D > 0$, we must have $f_{xx}(a, b)f_{yy}(a, b) > [f_{xy}(a, b)]^2 \ge 0$, so $f_{xx}$ and $f_{yy}$ have the same sign — meaning you can check either $f_{xx}$ or $f_{yy}$ in Cases 1 and 2.

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 946, Ex. 28 & Alhumaidy Notes): Classify the critical point of $z = e^{xy}$.

Set $f_x = y e^{xy} = 0$ and $f_y = x e^{xy} = 0$. Since $e^{xy} > 0$, the only critical point is $(0, 0)$. Computing second partials: $$f_{xx} = y^2 e^{xy}, \qquad f_{yy} = x^2 e^{xy}, \qquad f_{xy} = (1 + xy)e^{xy}$$ At $(0, 0)$: $f_{xx}(0, 0) = 0$, $f_{yy}(0, 0) = 0$, $f_{xy}(0, 0) = 1$, so $D = (0)(0) - 1^2 = -1 < 0$. Even though $f_{xx} = f_{yy} = 0$, $(0, 0, 1)$ is a saddle point!

Why It Works: Near $(a, b)$ where $f_x = f_y = 0$, the second-degree Taylor change is $\Delta f \approx \frac{1}{2}\big(f_{xx}h^2 + 2f_{xy}hk + f_{yy}k^2\big)$. Completing the square in $h$ (for $f_{xx} \neq 0$) gives: $$\Delta f \approx \frac{1}{2f_{xx}}\Big[\big(f_{xx}h + f_{xy}k\big)^2 + D\,k^2\Big]$$ When $D > 0$, the bracket is strictly positive for all $(h, k) \neq (0, 0)$, so $\Delta f$ always keeps the sign of $f_{xx}$. When $D < 0$, moving along $k = 0$ gives the sign of $f_{xx}$ while moving along $f_{xx}h + f_{xy}k = 0$ gives the opposite sign, producing a saddle.

Quick Check 2 (Textbook p. 947, Ex. 49): Suppose $f$ has continuous second partials near critical point $(3, 7)$, where $f_{xx}(3, 7) = 2$ and $f_{yy}(3, 7) = 8$. If $f$ has a relative minimum at $(3, 7)$ with $D > 0$, what is the interval of possible values for $f_{xy}(3, 7)$?
(A) $(-4, 4)$ (B) $(-\infty, -4) \cup (4, \infty)$ (C) $(-16, 16)$ (D) $(0, 4)$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (A) $(-4, 4)$. We require $D = f_{xx}(3, 7)f_{yy}(3, 7) - [f_{xy}(3, 7)]^2 > 0$, so $2(8) - [f_{xy}(3, 7)]^2 > 0 \implies [f_{xy}(3, 7)]^2 < 16 \implies -4 < f_{xy}(3, 7) < 4$.
Core Concept • §3

3. When the Second Partials Test Fails ($D = 0$ or Partials DNE)

Intuition: As Textbook p. 944 stresses, the Second Partials Test fails in two exact situations: (1) either first partial derivative does not exist at $(a, b)$, or (2) $D(a, b) = 0$. When $D = 0$, the surface could still be a bowl, a dome, or a saddle — you must go back to the definition of relative extrema and test the sign of $f(x, y) - f(a, b)$ directly around $(a, b)$.

Region where $f(x,y) - f(a,b) > 0$ Region where $f(x,y) - f(a,b) < 0$ Zero-level boundary $y = -x$

Both functions have $D = 0$ at $(0, 0)$, yet direct sign analysis shows $f(x, y) = x^2y^2$ has an absolute minimum along both axes (Textbook p. 944 Ex. 4) while $g(x, y) = x^3 + y^3$ has no extremum (Textbook p. 947 Ex. 35).

Direct Analysis Rules When $D = 0$ or Partials DNE:

  • Prove an extremum: Rewrite $f(x, y) - f(a, b)$ as a sum of squares, even powers, or clearly non-negative terms (e.g., $x^2 y^2 \ge 0$, $(x^2+y^2)^{1/3} \ge 0$, or $x^{2/3}+y^{2/3} \ge 0$ in Alhumaidy p. 947 Ex. 38) to prove $f(x, y) \ge f(a, b)$ or $f(x, y) \le f(a, b)$ on an open disk.
  • Disprove an extremum: Find two paths through $(a, b)$ (such as $y = x$ and $y = -x$, or positive vs. negative $t$) on which $f(x, y) - f(a, b)$ takes opposite signs arbitrarily close to $(a, b)$.

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 944, Example 4): Find the relative extrema of $f(x, y) = x^2 y^2$.

Here $f_x = 2xy^2 = 0$ and $f_y = 2x^2 y = 0$ hold whenever $x = 0$ or $y = 0$, so every point on the $x$-axis or $y$-axis is a critical point. Since $f_{xx} = 2y^2$, $f_{yy} = 2x^2$, and $f_{xy} = 4xy$, we get: $$D = (2y^2)(2x^2) - (4xy)^2 = -12x^2 y^2 = 0 \quad \text{whenever } x = 0 \text{ or } y = 0$$ Thus the Second Partials Test fails everywhere on both axes. However, $f(x, y) = 0$ at every point on either axis and $f(x, y) = x^2 y^2 > 0$ elsewhere, so every point on the $x$- and $y$-axes yields an absolute (and relative) minimum of $0$.

Why It Works: The Second Partials Test only checks quadratic (degree-2) curvature. When $D = 0$, higher-order terms (like $x^2y^2$ of degree 4 or $x^3+y^3$ of degree 3) control the surface shape, and direct comparison tests the exact definition of relative extrema without relying on second derivatives.

Quick Check 3 (Textbook p. 947, Ex. 35): For $f(x, y) = x^3 + y^3$, the only critical point is $(0, 0)$, where $D(0, 0) = 0$. What is true at $(0, 0)$?
(A) $f$ has a relative minimum at $(0, 0)$ (B) $f$ has a relative maximum at $(0, 0)$ (C) $f$ has neither a relative maximum nor a relative minimum at $(0, 0)$ (D) $(0, 0)$ is not a critical point because $D = 0$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (C) neither a relative maximum nor a relative minimum. Along the line $y = x$, $f(x, x) = 2x^3$ is positive for $x > 0$ and negative for $x < 0$, so every open disk centered at $(0, 0)$ contains points above and below $f(0, 0) = 0$.
Core Concept • §4

4. Absolute Extrema on Closed Bounded Regions

Intuition: Suppose you fence off a finite closed patch $R$ of the $xy$-plane (such as a rectangle, triangle, or parabolic lens containing all its border curves, Textbook p. 940 Figure 13.64). By the Extreme Value Theorem (Theorem 13.15), any continuous function $f(x, y)$ must reach an absolute maximum $M$ and an absolute minimum $m$ somewhere on $R$. Just like Calc I on $[a, b]$, those extreme values can happen at an interior critical point, along a boundary curve (found by 1D calculus after plugging in the curve’s equation), or at a corner vertex where two boundary curves meet (Textbook p. 945).

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): In handwritten solutions to Exercises 39, 42, and 43 (Alhumaidy PDF pp. 9–11), Dr. Alhumaidy enforces a strict 3-step exam routine: (1) always sketch $R$ and mark its corners; (2) cross out (outside $\times$) any critical point of $f$ or of a boundary edge that falls outside $R$; and (3) collect all surviving interior, boundary, and corner points in a single candidate table $(x_0, y_0) \mid f(x_0, y_0)$ to read off $M$ and $m$ without using $D$.
Interior critical point $(0, 1)$ Top edge $y=4$ & critical point $(0, 4)$ Parabolic edge $y=x^2$ & $(\pm\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4})$ Corners $(\pm 2, 4)$ attaining $M = 28$

Exact region $R$ bounded by $y = x^2$ and $y = 4$ for Textbook Ex. 43 / Alhumaidy p. 11 / KFUPM Final 242 Q11: testing interior, both boundary curves, and corners guarantees no extremum is missed.

3-Step Candidate Procedure (Textbook p. 940 Theorem 13.15 & p. 945): For a continuous function $f(x, y)$ on a closed bounded region $R$:

  1. Interior Critical Points: Solve $f_x = 0, f_y = 0$ (and check where partials DNE). Keep only points strictly inside $R$; discard any point outside $R$.
  2. Boundary Curve Critical Points: For each piece of the boundary (horizontal/vertical lines, slanted segments, or curves like $y = x^2$), substitute the boundary equation into $f(x, y)$ to obtain a 1-variable function $g(t)$ on a closed interval, then solve $g'(t) = 0$ (or DNE) inside that interval.
  3. Corners & Candidate Table: Collect all boundary intersection corners/endpoints together with the surviving points from Steps 1–2, evaluate $f(x, y)$ at every candidate, and read off the largest value (absolute maximum) and smallest value (absolute minimum).

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 945, Example 5): Find the absolute extrema of $f(x, y) = \sin xy$ on $0 \le x \le \pi$, $0 \le y \le 1$.

Setting $f_x = y\cos xy = 0$ and $f_y = x\cos xy = 0$ yields the interior critical point $(0, 0)$ (on the corner) and every point on the hyperbola $xy = \frac{\pi}{2}$ inside $R$, where $f(x, y) = \sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1$. On the four edges ($x = 0$, $x = \pi$, $y = 0$, $y = 1$): along $x = 0$ or $y = 0$, $f = 0$; along $y = 1$, $f(x, 1) = \sin x$ has $f'(\frac{\pi}{2}) = 0$ giving $(\frac{\pi}{2}, 1) \to 1$ and endpoints $(0,1), (\pi, 1) \to 0$; along $x = \pi$, $f(\pi, y) = \sin(\pi y)$ has $(\pi, \frac{1}{2}) \to 1$ and endpoints $(\pi, 0), (\pi, 1) \to 0$. Thus the absolute maximum is $1$ (along $xy = \frac{\pi}{2}$) and the absolute minimum is $0$ (along the axes and at $(\pi, 1)$).

Why It Works: A closed bounded region $R$ contains its boundary and fits inside a closed disk, so Theorem 13.15 guarantees $f$ attains both $M$ and $m$ on $R$. Any extremum in the open interior must satisfy Theorem 13.16 ($f_x = f_y = 0$ or DNE), while any extremum on a boundary arc is a 1D extremum on a closed interval, which occurs either at an endpoint (corner) or where the 1D derivative along that curve vanishes.

Quick Check 4 (Textbook p. 947, Ex. 39 / Alhumaidy p. 949 / Final 232 Q14): When finding the absolute extrema of $f(x, y) = x^2 - 4xy + 5$ on $R = \{(x, y): 1 \le x \le 4,\; 0 \le y \le 2\}$, what should you do with the critical point $(0, 0)$ obtained from $f_x = 0$ and $f_y = 0$?
(A) Test $(0, 0)$ with the Second Partials Test $D$ (B) Discard $(0, 0)$ because $(0, 0) \notin R$ (C) Include $(0, 0)$ in the candidate table because $f(0, 0) = 5$ (D) Replace $(0, 0)$ with $(1, 0)$ automatically
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) Discard $(0, 0)$ because $(0, 0) \notin R$. Since $R$ requires $1 \le x \le 4$, the point $(0, 0)$ lies outside the region and cannot be an extremum of $f$ on $R$.
Master Formulas

Section 13.8 Formula Reference & Edge Cases

Core Theorems, Classification Table & Hypotheses

  • Critical Points on an Open Region $R$: $(x_0, y_0) \in R$ is critical if: $$f_x(x_0, y_0) = 0 \text{ and } f_y(x_0, y_0) = 0, \qquad \text{OR} \qquad f_x(x_0, y_0) \text{ or } f_y(x_0, y_0) \text{ DNE.}$$
  • Second Partials Test (requires $f_x(a, b) = f_y(a, b) = 0$ and continuous second partials near $(a, b)$): $$D = f_{xx}(a, b)\,f_{yy}(a, b) - \big[f_{xy}(a, b)\big]^2$$
    • $D > 0$ and $f_{xx}(a, b) > 0$ (equivalently $f_{yy} > 0$) $\implies$ Relative Minimum at $(a, b)$ with value $f(a, b)$.
    • $D > 0$ and $f_{xx}(a, b) < 0$ (equivalently $f_{yy} < 0$) $\implies$ Relative Maximum at $(a, b)$ with value $f(a, b)$.
    • $D < 0$ $\implies$ Saddle Point at $\big(a, b, f(a, b)\big)$.
    • $D = 0$ $\implies$ Inconclusive (use direct inequality, completing the square, or 2-path test).
  • Extreme Value Theorem (Closed & Bounded $R$, $f$ Continuous on $R$): Absolute maximum $M$ and absolute minimum $m$ exist on $R$ and occur at either: (1) interior critical points in $R$, (2) 1D critical points along smooth boundary curves, or (3) corners/endpoints of boundary pieces.
  • Functions of $n$ Variables (Textbook p. 945): When all first partials of $w = f(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ exist, critical points satisfy $f_{x_1} = f_{x_2} = \dots = f_{x_n} = 0$ simultaneously (or where any partial DNE).
  • Quick Saddle Shortcut (Textbook p. 947, Ex. 50): If $f_{xx}(a, b)$ and $f_{yy}(a, b)$ have opposite signs at a critical point (or $f_{xx} = f_{yy} = 0$ with $f_{xy} \neq 0$), then $D < 0$ automatically — guaranteed saddle point!
Exam Traps

5 Classic Mistakes (WRONG vs. RIGHT)

Trap 1 — Calling a point critical when only ONE partial is zero:

WrongSetting $f_x = 0$ alone and listing all points on the $y$-axis for $1 - (x^2+y^2)^{1/3}$ as critical points.
RightRequire both $f_x = 0$ AND $f_y = 0$ simultaneously (or at least one partial DNE).

Trap 2 — Ignoring points where $f_x$ or $f_y$ does not exist (or plugging them into $D$):

WrongSaying $f(x, y) = (x^2 + y^2)^{1/3} + 2$ has no extrema because $f_x = 0, f_y = 0$ has no solution.
RightCheck where denominators vanish: $(0, 0)$ is critical (partials DNE), and $(x^2+y^2)^{1/3} \ge 0$ gives a rel. min directly.

Trap 3 — Confusing $D > 0$ signs or ignoring $-[f_{xy}]^2$:

WrongConcluding $f_{xx} > 0, f_{yy} > 0 \implies$ relative minimum without computing $D$, or thinking $f_{xx} > 0$ means maximum.
RightAlways compute $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - [f_{xy}]^2$: $D > 0, f_{xx} > 0 \implies$ min (cup up); $D > 0, f_{xx} < 0 \implies$ max (cup down); $D < 0 \implies$ saddle.

Trap 4 — Including interior critical points that lie outside $R$:

WrongEvaluating $f(0, 0) = 5$ in the absolute extrema table for $R = \{(x, y) : 1 \le x \le 4,\; 0 \le y \le 2\}$.
RightVerify every critical point against ALL inequalities defining $R$ (here $x = 0 < 1$, so $(0, 0) \notin R$ and must be rejected).

Trap 5 — Only checking corners of $R$ and skipping boundary interior critical points:

WrongPlugging only the 4 rectangle corners into $f(x, y) = x^2 + xy$ on $|x| \le 2, |y| \le 1$ (missing $m = -\frac{1}{4}$!).
RightSubstitute each edge equation into $f$ (e.g., $y=1 \implies x^2+x$), solve $g'(t) = 0$, and add those edge points to the candidate table.
Worked Examples

From Textbook Basics to KFUPM Final Level

Example 1 • Second Partials Test • Textbook p. 944 Example 3 & Alhumaidy Notes

Finding Relative Extrema and Saddle Points via the $D$-Table

Find all relative extrema and saddle points of $f(x, y) = -x^3 + 4xy - 2y^2 + 1$.
Final Answer: Saddle point at $(0, 0, 1)$; relative maximum at $\left(\dfrac{4}{3}, \dfrac{4}{3}\right)$ with value $f\!\left(\dfrac{4}{3}, \dfrac{4}{3}\right) = \dfrac{59}{27}$.
1
Solve $f_x = 0$ and $f_y = 0$ for Critical Points

Because $f$ is a polynomial, $f_x$ and $f_y$ exist everywhere:

$$\begin{cases} f_x(x, y) = -3x^2 + 4y = 0 & (1) \\ f_y(x, y) = 4x - 4y = 0 & (2) \end{cases}$$

From $(2)$, $4(x - y) = 0 \implies y = x$. Substitute $y = x$ into $(1)$:

$$-3x^2 + 4x = 0 \implies x(4 - 3x) = 0 \implies x = 0 \quad \text{or} \quad x = \frac{4}{3}$$

Since $y = x$, the two critical points are $(0, 0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{4}{3}, \dfrac{4}{3}\right)$.

2
Compute Second Partials & Build Dr. Alhumaidy’s $D$-Table
$$f_{xx}(x, y) = -6x, \qquad f_{yy}(x, y) = -4, \qquad f_{xy}(x, y) = 4$$ $$D(x, y) = f_{xx}f_{yy} - (f_{xy})^2 = (-6x)(-4) - 4^2 = 24x - 16$$
  • At $(0, 0)$: $f_{xx} = 0$, $f_{yy} = -4$, $f_{xy} = 4 \implies D = 0(-4) - 16 = -16 < 0 \implies$ Saddle point at $(0, 0, 1)$.
  • At $\left(\dfrac{4}{3}, \dfrac{4}{3}\right)$: $f_{xx} = -8$, $f_{yy} = -4$, $f_{xy} = 4 \implies D = (-8)(-4) - 16 = 16 > 0$. Since $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} = -8 < 0 \implies$ Relative maximum.

Evaluate the maximum value:

$$f\!\left(\frac{4}{3}, \frac{4}{3}\right) = -\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^3 + 4\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2 - 2\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2 + 1 = -\frac{64}{27} + \frac{32}{9} + 1 = \frac{-64 + 96 + 27}{27} = \frac{59}{27}$$
Verification: Along the line $y = x$, $g(x) = f(x, x) = -x^3 + 2x^2 + 1$ has $g'(x) = -3x^2 + 4x$ and $g''(x) = -6x + 4$, so $g''(\frac{4}{3}) = -4 < 0$ (concave down at the maximum) while $g''(0) = 4 > 0$ (concave up along $y=x$, opposite to $f_{yy}=-4 < 0$ along $x=0$, confirming the saddle at $(0, 0)$).
Example 2 • Nonlinear Critical-Point System • KFUPM Final Term 253 Q12

Eliminating Cross Terms to Find Two Saddle Points

Determine the number and type of relative extrema and saddle points of the function $f(x, y) = 4 + x - y - x^2 y + x y^2$.
Final Answer: The graph of $f$ has two saddle points, at $(1, 1)$ and $(-1, -1)$, and no relative extrema.
1
Set First Partial Derivatives to Zero and Add Equations
$$\begin{cases} f_x(x, y) = 1 - 2xy + y^2 = 0 & (1) \\ f_y(x, y) = -1 - x^2 + 2xy = 0 & (2) \end{cases}$$

Adding $(1)$ and $(2)$ cancels both the constants and $\pm 2xy$:

$$(1 - 2xy + y^2) + (-1 - x^2 + 2xy) = 0 \implies y^2 - x^2 = 0 \implies (y - x)(y + x) = 0$$
2
Solve Both Cases $y = x$ and $y = -x$
  • Case 1 ($y = x$): Substitute into $(1)$: $1 - 2x^2 + x^2 = 0 \implies 1 - x^2 = 0 \implies x = \pm 1$. This gives $(1, 1)$ and $(-1, -1)$ (both satisfy $(2)$).
  • Case 2 ($y = -x$): Substitute into $(1)$: $1 - 2x(-x) + (-x)^2 = 0 \implies 1 + 3x^2 = 0$, which has no real solution since $1 + 3x^2 \ge 1 > 0$.
3
Apply the Second Partials Test
$$f_{xx} = -2y, \qquad f_{yy} = 2x, \qquad f_{xy} = -2x + 2y$$ $$D(x, y) = (-2y)(2x) - (-2x + 2y)^2 = -4xy - 4(y - x)^2$$
  • At $(1, 1)$: $D(1, 1) = -4(1)(1) - 0 = -4 < 0 \implies$ Saddle point.
  • At $(-1, -1)$: $D(-1, -1) = -4(-1)(-1) - 0 = -4 < 0 \implies$ Saddle point.
Verification: At $(1, 1)$, $f_{xx} = -2 < 0$ and $f_{yy} = 2 > 0$; at $(-1, -1)$, $f_{xx} = 2 > 0$ and $f_{yy} = -2 < 0$. Because $f_{xx}$ and $f_{yy}$ have opposite signs at both critical points, $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - [f_{xy}]^2$ is guaranteed negative!
Example 3 • Four Critical Points • KFUPM Final Term 252 Q10

Factored Partial Derivatives Yielding Mixed Critical Points

Classify all critical points of $f(x, y) = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 - x^2 + (x - 1)y^2$.
Final Answer: The graph has two saddle points at $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$, one relative maximum at $(0, 0)$, and one relative minimum at $(2, 0)$.
1
Factor $f_y = 0$ Carefully to Avoid Missing Branches
$$f_x(x, y) = x^2 - 2x + y^2 = 0, \qquad f_y(x, y) = 2(x - 1)y = 0$$

From $2(x - 1)y = 0$, either $y = 0$ OR $x = 1$:

  • If $y = 0$: $f_x = x^2 - 2x = x(x - 2) = 0 \implies x = 0$ or $x = 2$, giving $(0, 0)$ and $(2, 0)$.
  • If $x = 1$: $f_x = 1 - 2 + y^2 = 0 \implies y^2 = 1 \implies y = \pm 1$, giving $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$.
2
Classify All Four Critical Points via $D$
$$f_{xx} = 2(x - 1), \qquad f_{yy} = 2(x - 1), \qquad f_{xy} = 2y$$ $$D(x, y) = 4(x - 1)^2 - 4y^2$$
  • At $(0, 0)$: $D = 4(-1)^2 - 0 = 4 > 0$ and $f_{xx}(0, 0) = -2 < 0 \implies$ Relative maximum.
  • At $(2, 0)$: $D = 4(1)^2 - 0 = 4 > 0$ and $f_{xx}(2, 0) = 2 > 0 \implies$ Relative minimum.
  • At $(1, 1)$: $D = 0 - 4(1)^2 = -4 < 0 \implies$ Saddle point.
  • At $(1, -1)$: $D = 0 - 4(-1)^2 = -4 < 0 \implies$ Saddle point.
Verification: Along $y = 0$, $f(x, 0) = \frac{1}{3}x^3 - x^2$ indeed has a local max at $x = 0$ and local min at $x = 2$; at $(1, \pm 1)$, $f_{xx} = f_{yy} = 0$ while $f_{xy} = \pm 2 \neq 0$, ensuring $D = -[f_{xy}]^2 = -4 < 0$.
Example 4 • Curved Boundary Region • Textbook p. 947 Ex. 43, Alhumaidy Notes p. 11 & Final 242 Q11

Absolute Extrema on the Parabolic Region $y = x^2$ to $y = 4$

Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of $f(x, y) = 3x^2 + 2y^2 - 4y$ over the closed region $R$ in the $xy$-plane bounded by the graphs of $y = x^2$ and $y = 4$. (KFUPM Final 242 Q11 asks for the maximum value.)
Final Answer: Absolute maximum $M = 28$ at $(-2, 4)$ and $(2, 4)$; absolute minimum $m = -2$ at $(0, 1)$.
1
Describe Region $R$ & Check Interior Critical Points

Setting $x^2 = 4$ gives corners $(-2, 4)$ and $(2, 4)$, so $R = \{(x, y) : -2 \le x \le 2,\; x^2 \le y \le 4\}$ (shown in §4 Diagram). Inside $R$:

$$f_x = 6x = 0 \implies x = 0, \qquad f_y = 4y - 4 = 0 \implies y = 1$$

Since $0^2 = 0 < 1 < 4$, $(0, 1)$ is strictly inside $R$ with $f(0, 1) = 0 + 2 - 4 = -2$.

2
Optimize $f$ Along Both Boundary Curves
  • Top segment ($y = 4$, $-2 \le x \le 2$): $$g_1(x) = f(x, 4) = 3x^2 + 2(16) - 4(4) = 3x^2 + 16$$ $g_1'(x) = 6x = 0 \implies x = 0$, giving $(0, 4)$ with $f(0, 4) = 16$. Endpoints $x = \pm 2$ give $f(\pm 2, 4) = 3(4) + 16 = 28$.
  • Parabolic arc ($y = x^2$, $-2 \le x \le 2$): $$g_2(x) = f(x, x^2) = 3x^2 + 2x^4 - 4x^2 = 2x^4 - x^2$$ $g_2'(x) = 8x^3 - 2x = 2x(4x^2 - 1) = 0 \implies x = 0$ or $x = \pm \dfrac{1}{2}$ (all in $[-2, 2]$). Thus $(0, 0) \to 0$ and $\left(\pm\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{4}\right) \to 2\left(\dfrac{1}{16}\right) - \dfrac{1}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{8}$.
3
Compare All Candidates in a Table

Comparing $f(0, 1) = -2$, $f\!\left(\pm\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}\right) = -\frac{1}{8}$, $f(0, 0) = 0$, $f(0, 4) = 16$, and $f(\pm 2, 4) = 28$: the absolute maximum is $M = 28$ and the absolute minimum is $m = -2$.

Verification: Completing the square gives $f(x, y) = 3x^2 + 2(y - 1)^2 - 2$. Thus $f(x, y) \ge -2$ everywhere (confirming $m = -2$ at $(0, 1)$), while on $R$ we have $|x| \le 2$ and $|y - 1| \le 3$, bounded above by $3(4) + 2(9) - 2 = 28$, achieved exactly at $(\pm 2, 4)$.
Example 5 • Triangular Region & Critical Line • Textbook p. 947 Ex. 42, Alhumaidy Notes p. 10 & Final 241 Q10

Absolute Extrema of $f(x, y) = (2x - y)^2$ on a Triangle

Let $T$ be the closed triangular region in the $xy$-plane with vertices $(2, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, and $(1, 2)$. If $M$ and $m$ are the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of $f(x, y) = (2x - y)^2$ over $T$, find $M + m$.
Final Answer: $M = 16$ at $(2, 0)$ and $m = 0$ along the segment of $y = 2x$ inside $T$, so $M + m = 16$.
1
Find the Interior Critical Line $y = 2x$
$$f_x = 4(2x - y) = 0, \qquad f_y = -2(2x - y) = 0 \implies y = 2x$$

Every point on the line $y = 2x$ is a critical point giving $f(x, 2x) = (2x - 2x)^2 = 0$. Notice that the vertex $(1, 2)$ lies on this line, and $y = 2x$ slices right through the interior of $T$!

2
Parameterize All Three Triangle Edges ($S_1, S_2, S_3$)
  • Edge $S_1$ from $(2, 0)$ to $(1, 2)$: Slope $\dfrac{2 - 0}{1 - 2} = -2 \implies y = -2x + 4$ ($1 \le x \le 2$). $$g_1(x) = \big(2x - (-2x + 4)\big)^2 = (4x - 4)^2 \implies g_1'(x) = 32x - 32 = 0 \implies x = 1,\; y = 2$$
  • Edge $S_2$ from $(0, 1)$ to $(1, 2)$: Slope $\dfrac{2 - 1}{1 - 0} = 1 \implies y = x + 1$ ($0 \le x \le 1$). $$g_2(x) = \big(2x - (x + 1)\big)^2 = (x - 1)^2 \implies g_2'(x) = 2(x - 1) = 0 \implies x = 1,\; y = 2$$
  • Edge $S_3$ from $(2, 0)$ to $(0, 1)$: Slope $\dfrac{1 - 0}{0 - 2} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \implies y = -\dfrac{1}{2}x + 1$ ($0 \le x \le 2$). $$g_3(x) = \left(2x - \left(-\frac{1}{2}x + 1\right)\right)^2 = \left(\frac{5}{2}x - 1\right)^2$$ $$g_3'(x) = 2\left(\frac{5}{2}x - 1\right)\left(\frac{5}{2}\right) = \frac{25}{2}x - 5 = 0 \implies x = \frac{2}{5},\; y = -\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2}{5}\right) + 1 = \frac{4}{5}$$ At $\left(\dfrac{2}{5}, \dfrac{4}{5}\right)$, we have $y = 2x$, so $f\!\left(\dfrac{2}{5}, \dfrac{4}{5}\right) = 0$.
3
Compare All Candidates and Compute $M + m$

Candidate values: $f(1, 2) = 0$, $f(0, 1) = (0 - 1)^2 = 1$, $f(2, 0) = (4 - 0)^2 = 16$, $f\!\left(\frac{2}{5}, \frac{4}{5}\right) = 0$, and $f(x, 2x) = 0$ on $y = 2x$ inside $T$. Thus $M = 16$, $m = 0$, and $M + m = 16$.

Triangular region $T$ and edges $S_1, S_2, S_3$ Critical line $y = 2x$ (attains $m = 0$) Vertex $(2, 0)$ (attains $M = 16$)

Exact geometry of Example 5 (Alhumaidy p. 10 / Final 241 Q10): the critical line $y = 2x$ enters $T$ at $(\frac{2}{5}, \frac{4}{5})$ on $S_3$ and exits at $(1, 2)$, giving $m = 0$, while the farthest vertex $(2, 0)$ achieves $M = 16$.

Verification: Since $f(x, y) = (2x - y)^2 \ge 0$ everywhere and $y = 2x$ intersects $T$, $m = 0$ is immediate. On any line segment, $2x - y$ is linear, so $|2x - y|$ is maximized at one of the three vertices: $|4-0|=4$, $|0-1|=1$, $|2-2|=0$, confirming $M = 4^2 = 16$.
One-Screen Summary

The 5 Things to Know for the Exam

  1. Critical points require BOTH partials $= 0$ OR at least one partial DNE: Never stop after solving $f_x = 0$ alone, and always inspect denominators and fractional powers like $(x^2+y^2)^{1/3}$ where partials fail to exist.
  2. Use Dr. Alhumaidy’s $D$-table ($D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - [f_{xy}]^2$): At every smooth critical point, $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} > 0$ gives a relative minimum; $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} < 0$ gives a relative maximum; $D < 0$ gives a saddle point.
  3. When $D = 0$ or partials DNE, switch immediately to direct comparison: Check whether $f(x, y) - f(a, b)$ keeps a fixed sign near $(a, b)$ (using squares/roots) or changes sign along two paths through $(a, b)$.
  4. For absolute extrema on a closed bounded region $R$, sketch $R$ first: Keep only interior critical points strictly inside $R$, substitute every boundary curve to find 1D critical points along each edge, and put all corners into one candidate table.
  5. Read KFUPM MCQ targets carefully: Check whether the question asks for the number of saddles/maxima/minima, the extreme value $M$ or $m$, or a combination like $M + m$.

13.9 Applications of Extrema
