Unlocking $\sqrt{1 + y^3}$ by Switching from $dy\,dx$ to $dx\,dy$

Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_0^2 \int_x^2 x\sqrt{1 + y^3}\,dy\,dx$.
Final Answer: $\dfrac{26}{9}$.
1
Recognize Why Reversal Is Required and Sketch $R$

Holding $x$ constant, $\sqrt{1 + y^3}$ has no elementary antiderivative in $y$. From the limits $0 \le x \le 2$ and $x \le y \le 2$, $R$ is the upper-left triangle with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(0, 2)$, and $(2, 2)$, bounded below by $y = x$, above by $y = 2$, and on the left by $x = 0$.

2
Re-Slice Horizontally ($dx\,dy$)

Across $R$, $y$ spans $0 \le y \le 2$. For each fixed $y$, a horizontal arrow enters at the $y$-axis ($x = 0$) and exits at the line $y = x$ ($x = y$):

$$\int_0^2 \int_x^2 x\sqrt{1 + y^3}\,dy\,dx = \int_0^2 \int_0^y x\sqrt{1 + y^3}\,dx\,dy$$
3
Integrate wrt $x$ First, Then Use $u = 1 + y^3$
$$\int_0^y x\sqrt{1 + y^3}\,dx = \sqrt{1 + y^3}\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_{x=0}^{x=y} = \frac{1}{2}y^2\sqrt{1 + y^3}$$

Now substitute $u = 1 + y^3$, so $du = 3y^2\,dy \implies y^2\,dy = \frac{1}{3}\,du$, with $y=0 \implies u=1$ and $y=2 \implies u=9$:

$$\frac{1}{2}\int_0^2 y^2\sqrt{1 + y^3}\,dy = \frac{1}{6}\int_1^9 u^{1/2}\,du = \frac{1}{6}\left[\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_1^9 = \frac{1}{9}\left(9^{3/2} - 1^{3/2}\right) = \frac{1}{9}(27 - 1) = \frac{26}{9}$$
Verification: Differentiate $\frac{1}{9}(1+y^3)^{3/2}$ wrt $y$: $\frac{1}{9}\cdot\frac{3}{2}(1+y^3)^{1/2}\cdot 3y^2 = \frac{1}{2}y^2\sqrt{1+y^3}$, matching the inner integral. Moreover, on $0 \le y \le 2$, $1 \le \sqrt{1+y^3} \le 3$ and $\int_0^2 \frac{1}{2}y^2\,dy = \frac{4}{3}$, so the answer must lie in $\left[\frac{4}{3}, 4\right]$; indeed $\frac{4}{3} < \frac{26}{9} \approx 2.89 < 4$.
Example 5 • Quadrant III Reversal & Sign Selection • KFUPM Final Term 252 Q15

Reversing Order on a Negative-Coordinate Region

Reverse the order of integration for $\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{0} \int_{4x}^{-4x^2} f(x, y)\,dy\,dx$.
Final Answer: $\displaystyle \int_{-4}^{0} \int_{-\sqrt{-y/4}}^{y/4} f(x, y)\,dx\,dy$.
1
Locate the Quadrant and Find Corner Intersections

The given $dy\,dx$ limits are $-1 \le x \le 0$ and $4x \le y \le -4x^2$. Notice that for $x \in [-1, 0]$, both $4x \le 0$ and $-4x^2 \le 0$, so $R$ lies entirely in Quadrant III ($x \le 0$ and $y \le 0$). Set the lower and upper curves equal:

$$4x = -4x^2 \implies 4x(x + 1) = 0 \implies x = 0 \text{ or } x = -1$$

Thus the corners are $(0, 0)$ and $(-1, -4)$, and $y$ spans $-4 \le y \le 0$.

2
Invert Both Boundary Curves With the Quadrant III Sign
  • Line $y = 4x$: Solving for $x$ gives $x = \dfrac{y}{4}$.
  • Parabola $y = -4x^2$: Solving for $x^2$ gives $x^2 = -\dfrac{y}{4}$ (note $-\frac{y}{4} \ge 0$ because $y \le 0$). Since $x \le 0$ in Quadrant III, we MUST take the negative root: $$x = -\sqrt{-\frac{y}{4}}$$
3
Determine Left vs. Right Bounds Using a Horizontal Slice

Test $y = -1$ (or $y = -1.44$ in Diagram 5): on the parabola, $x = -\sqrt{1/4} = -\frac{1}{2}$; on the line, $x = -\frac{1}{4}$. Because $-\frac{1}{2} < -\frac{1}{4}$, the parabola is on the left and the line is on the right:

$$\int_{-1}^{0} \int_{4x}^{-4x^2} f(x, y)\,dy\,dx = \int_{-4}^{0} \int_{-\sqrt{-y/4}}^{y/4} f(x, y)\,dx\,dy$$
Left boundary $x = -\sqrt{-y/4}$ (in Q-III, $x \le 0$) Right boundary $x = y/4$ Horizontal slice ($dx\,dy$) at fixed $y \in [-4, 0]$

Exact Quadrant III geometry of KFUPM Final 252 Q15: because $x \le 0$ throughout $R$, $y = -4x^2$ solves to $x = -\sqrt{-y/4}$, which sits strictly to the left of $x = y/4$.

Verification: Compute the area ($f(x,y) = 1$) in both orders: original order gives $\int_{-1}^0 (-4x^2 - 4x)\,dx = \left[-\frac{4}{3}x^3 - 2x^2\right]_{-1}^0 = -\left(\frac{4}{3} - 2\right) = \frac{2}{3}$; reversed order gives $\int_{-4}^0 \left(\frac{y}{4} + \frac{1}{2}(-y)^{1/2}\right)dy = \left[\frac{y^2}{8} - \frac{1}{3}(-y)^{3/2}\right]_{-4}^0 = -\left(2 - \frac{8}{3}\right) = \frac{2}{3}$. Both yield the exact same positive area $\frac{2}{3}$.
One-Screen Summary

The 5 Things to Know for the Exam

  1. Integrate inside-out and keep outer bounds constant: Hold the outer variable fixed during the inner integration; the inner result depends only on the outer variable, and the outer limits must always be constants.
  2. Match slice direction to integration order: $dy\,dx$ scans vertically ($\uparrow$, inner limits $y_{\text{bottom}}(x)$ to $y_{\text{top}}(x)$); $dx\,dy$ scans horizontally ($\rightarrow$, inner limits $x_{\text{left}}(y)$ to $x_{\text{right}}(y)$).
  3. Never reverse variable limits without sketching first: Plot all bounding curves, locate every corner intersection, and check which quadrant $R$ sits in so square roots ($x = \pm\sqrt{\cdot}$ or $y = \pm\sqrt{\cdot}$) get the right sign.
  4. Spot non-elementary integrands immediately: Seeing $e^{\pm y^2}$, $\cos(y^2)$, $\sin(x^2)$, $\sqrt{1+y^3}$, or $\frac{1}{2+y^3}$ on the inner integral is your green light to reverse the order of integration (not to force an antiderivative!).
  5. Exploit rectangle separability and splitting/merging: Over constant rectangular limits, a product $p(x)q(y)$ splits into $\left(\int p(x)\,dx\right)\left(\int q(y)\,dy\right)$, and a region split into two integrals in one order often merges into one integral in the reverse order.
CONCEPT MASTERCLASS • SECTION 14.2

14.2 Double Integrals and Volume

Larson & Edwards 7e (pp. 978–989) & Dr. Alhumaidy Notes — Volume Under and Between Surfaces, Fubini’s Theorem & Reversing Integration Order, Properties, Symmetry & Bounds, and Average Value Over a Region.

Jump to section:
Lecture Video • 14.2 Double Integrals & Volume
14.2 Volumes Under Surfaces (14:43) — Covers computing 3D volumes under and between surfaces by projecting onto the $xy$-plane.
Watch on YouTube ↗
Full topic lecture by Eng. Anas Abu Zahra (video has no chapter/caption index for timestamps).

What You Already Know

In Calculus I and II, the definite integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ arises as the limit of Riemann sums $\sum f(x_i)\,\Delta x_i$ and measures signed area, average value $\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, and volume by cross sections $\int_a^b A(x)\,dx$. In Section 14.1, you learned how to evaluate iterated integrals over a 2D region $R$ by holding one variable fixed while integrating the other, and how to read a region vertically ($dy\,dx$) or horizontally ($dx\,dy$). Section 14.2 connects those iterated integrals to true 3D volume, symmetry shortcuts, order reversal on non-elementary integrands, and 2D average value.

Core Concept • §1

1. Double Integrals & Volume Under or Between Surfaces

Intuition: Imagine building a 3D solid standing over a flat floor region $R$ in the $xy$-plane and capped by a roof surface $z = f(x, y) \ge 0$ (Textbook pp. 978–980, Figures 14.8–14.11). Cover $R$ with a grid of tiny rectangles inside $R$ (an inner partition $\Delta$ whose norm $\|\Delta\|$ is the longest diagonal). Above each rectangle of area $\Delta A_i$, erect a vertical rectangular prism of height $f(x_i, y_i)$ and volume $f(x_i, y_i)\,\Delta A_i$. Shrinking the grid ($\|\Delta\| \to 0$) turns the sum of prism volumes into the exact double integral. When the solid sits between a ceiling $z_{\text{top}}$ and a floor $z_{\text{bottom}}$, each prism simply has height $\Delta z = z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}}$.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Larson (Textbook p. 985, Example 5) computes the volume between two surfaces as $(\text{volume under upper surface}) - (\text{volume under lower surface})$ and then combines the two double integrals. Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes (pp. 983, 988 Ex. 35 & 39) write $\iint_R \Delta z\,dA$ directly, where $\Delta z = z_{\text{upper}} - z_{\text{lower}}$ is formed immediately after setting $z_1 = z_2$ to find the projection shadow $R$ in the $xy$-plane.
Upper surface $z_{\text{top}} = 4 - x^2 - y^2$ & shadow circle Lower plane $z_{\text{bot}} = 4 - 2x$ Vertical column height $\Delta z = 2x - x^2 - y^2$ Representative slice $dy\,dx$ over $R$

Equating $z_{\text{top}} = z_{\text{bot}}$ projects the 3D seam onto the $xy$-plane disk $(x-1)^2 + y^2 \le 1$, and integrating $\Delta z = z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bot}}$ over $R$ gives the exact enclosed volume (Textbook p. 988, Ex. 35).

Definitions & Formulas (Textbook p. 980 & p. 985):

  • Double Integral (Riemann Sum Limit): If $f$ is defined on a closed, bounded plane region $R$, then $$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \lim_{\|\Delta\| \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i, y_i)\,\Delta A_i$$ provided this limit exists (for example, whenever $f$ is continuous on a union of finitely many nonoverlapping vertically/horizontally simple regions).
  • Volume Under One Surface ($z = f(x, y) \ge 0$ on $R$): $$V = \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$$
  • Volume Between Two Surfaces ($z_{\text{bottom}}(x, y) \le z_{\text{top}}(x, y)$ on $R$): $$V = \iint_R \big(z_{\text{top}}(x, y) - z_{\text{bottom}}(x, y)\big)\,dA$$ When the shadow $R$ is not explicitly given, equate $z_{\text{top}} = z_{\text{bottom}}$ to find the boundary curve of $R$ in the $xy$-plane, then test an interior point of $R$ to confirm which surface is on top.

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 987, Ex. 21 & Alhumaidy Notes): Find the volume of the solid under the plane $z = \frac{y}{2}$ above the rectangle $0 \le x \le 4,\; 0 \le y \le 2$.

Since $\frac{y}{2} \ge 0$ on the rectangle, we integrate directly: $$V = \int_0^4 \int_0^2 \frac{y}{2}\,dy\,dx = \int_0^4 \left[\frac{y^2}{4}\right]_{y=0}^{y=2} dx = \int_0^4 1\,dx = 4.$$

Why It Works (Cross-Sectional Sweeping, Textbook p. 981, Figures 14.14–14.16): Holding $x$ fixed and integrating $\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy$ sweeps a vertical rod across the slice to compute the cross-sectional area $A(x)$ parallel to the $yz$-plane. Integrating $\int_a^b A(x)\,dx$ then sweeps that cross section from $x = a$ to $x = b$ to accumulate the entire 3D volume.

Quick Check 1 (Textbook p. 987, Ex. 22): What is the volume of the solid below $z = 6 - 2y$ and above the rectangle $0 \le x \le 4,\; 0 \le y \le 2$ in the $xy$-plane?
(A) $16$ (B) $24$ (C) $32$ (D) $8$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (C) $32$. For $0 \le y \le 2$, $6 - 2y \ge 2 > 0$. Integrate: $\int_0^4 \int_0^2 (6 - 2y)\,dy\,dx = \int_0^4 [6y - y^2]_0^2\,dx = \int_0^4 (12 - 4)\,dx = 8(4) = 32$.
Core Concept • §2

2. Fubini’s Theorem & Reversing the Order of Integration

Intuition: Unlike single integrals, where difficulty depends almost entirely on the integrand $f(x)$, a double integral’s difficulty depends heavily on which direction you slice $R$ (Textbook pp. 982–984). Sometimes slicing horizontally ($dx\,dy$) instead of vertically ($dy\,dx$) avoids splitting $R$ into two pieces (Alhumaidy notes p. 987, Ex. 19), and other times the inner integral has no elementary antiderivative at all (such as $\int e^{-x^2}\,dx$, $\int e^{y^2}\,dy$, $\int \sin(y^2)\,dy$, or $\int \frac{1}{1+x^4}\,dx$) until you reverse the order of integration.

Vertical slice $dy\,dx$: bottom $y=0$ to top $y=x$ Horizontal slice $dx\,dy$: left $x=y$ to right $x=1$ Inner integration sweep direction

Both iterated integrals describe the exact same triangle (Textbook p. 984, Example 4), yet $dy\,dx$ evaluates $e^{-x^2}$ cleanly while $dx\,dy$ hits a non-elementary integral $\int e^{-x^2}\,dx$.

Theorem 14.2 — Fubini’s Theorem (Textbook p. 982): Let $f$ be continuous on a plane region $R$.

  1. Vertically simple ($dy\,dx$): If $R$ is defined by $a \le x \le b$ and $g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)$ with $g_1, g_2$ continuous on $[a, b]$, then $$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy\,dx.$$
  2. Horizontally simple ($dx\,dy$): If $R$ is defined by $c \le y \le d$ and $h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)$ with $h_1, h_2$ continuous on $[c, d]$, then $$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x, y)\,dx\,dy.$$

3-Step Reversal Recipe (Inside Any General Double Integral):

  1. Read the inequalities from the limits: inner limits give the first variable between two curves; outer limits give the second variable between two constants.
  2. Sketch $R$ and find all corner intersections (so you know the global min/max of both $x$ and $y$).
  3. Re-slice in the perpendicular direction: place constant bounds on the outside and solve the boundary curves for the inner variable (left-to-right for $dx\,dy$, bottom-to-top for $dy\,dx$).

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 988, Ex. 45 & Alhumaidy Notes): Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \int_{y/2}^{1/2} e^{-x^2}\,dx\,dy$.

Since $\int e^{-x^2}\,dx$ is non-elementary, reverse the order. The region is $0 \le y \le 1$, $\frac{y}{2} \le x \le \frac{1}{2}$ — the triangle bounded by $y = 0$, $x = \frac{1}{2}$, and $y = 2x$, with vertices $(0, 0)$, $\left(\frac{1}{2}, 0\right)$, and $\left(\frac{1}{2}, 1\right)$. Slicing vertically ($dy\,dx$) gives $0 \le x \le \frac{1}{2}$ and $0 \le y \le 2x$: $$\int_0^{1/2} \int_0^{2x} e^{-x^2}\,dy\,dx = \int_0^{1/2} 2x e^{-x^2}\,dx = \Big[-e^{-x^2}\Big]_0^{1/2} = 1 - e^{-1/4}.$$

Why It Works: Both iterated integrals accumulate the same signed volume (or general continuous function mass) over the exact same 2D region $R$; only the order of slicing changes. When $f$ is continuous on $R$, Fubini’s Theorem guarantees both orders yield the exact same value.

Quick Check 2 (Textbook p. 988, Ex. 49): When you reverse the order of integration in $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \int_{2x}^4 \sin(y^2)\,dy\,dx$, which iterated integral do you obtain?
(A) $\displaystyle\int_0^4 \int_0^{y/2} \sin(y^2)\,dx\,dy$ (B) $\displaystyle\int_0^4 \int_{y/2}^2 \sin(y^2)\,dx\,dy$ (C) $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \int_0^{y/2} \sin(y^2)\,dx\,dy$ (D) $\displaystyle\int_{2x}^4 \int_0^2 \sin(y^2)\,dx\,dy$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (A). The region $0 \le x \le 2$, $2x \le y \le 4$ is the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(0,4)$, and $(2,4)$. Slicing horizontally gives $0 \le y \le 4$ and $0 \le x \le \frac{y}{2}$, producing $\int_0^4 \frac{y}{2}\sin(y^2)\,dy = \frac{1}{4}(1 - \cos 16)$.
Core Concept • §3

3. Properties of Double Integrals, Symmetry & Bounds

Intuition: Before cranking through an iterated integral, check if linearity, domain splitting, odd/even symmetry, or a quick upper/lower bound can solve or simplify the problem immediately (Textbook pp. 980, 987–989). On a region symmetric across an axis, every point $(x, y)$ has a twin $(-x, y)$ or $(x, -y)$: if the integrand has opposite signs at those twins (odd symmetry), their contributions cancel to zero; if it has the same value (even symmetry), you can integrate over half the region and double the answer.

Symmetric domain $R$ Actual integral $\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA$ Lower bound $m\cdot\text{Area}(R)$ Upper bound $M\cdot\text{Area}(R)$

Symmetry cancels odd terms over symmetric regions (Textbook p. 987, Ex. 11), while monotonicity sandwiches any integral between the flat slabs of its minimum $m$ and maximum $M$ (Textbook p. 989, Ex. 65).

Theorem 14.1 & Key Consequences (Textbook pp. 980, 988–989): Let $f, g$ be continuous on a closed, bounded region $R$ with area $A = \iint_R dA$.

  • Linearity: $\iint_R c\,f(x, y)\,dA = c\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$ and $\iint_R [f(x, y) \pm g(x, y)]\,dA = \iint_R f\,dA \pm \iint_R g\,dA$.
  • Nonnegativity & Comparison (Monotonicity): If $f \ge 0$ on $R$, then $\iint_R f\,dA \ge 0$; if $f(x, y) \ge g(x, y)$ on $R$, then $\iint_R f\,dA \ge \iint_R g\,dA$.
  • Bounding Estimate (Ex. 60, 65): If $m \le f(x, y) \le M$ on $R$, then $$m\cdot\text{Area}(R) \le \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA \le M\cdot\text{Area}(R).$$ In particular, for a constant height $f(x, y) = k$, $\iint_R k\,dA = k\cdot\text{Area}(R)$ (Ex. 59).
  • Domain Additivity: If $R = R_1 \cup R_2$ where $R_1$ and $R_2$ overlap only along a boundary of area $0$, then $\iint_R f\,dA = \iint_{R_1} f\,dA + \iint_{R_2} f\,dA$.
  • Odd/Even Symmetry (Both $R$ and $f$ Must Be Symmetric!): If $R$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis ($(x, y) \in R \iff (-x, y) \in R$), then: $$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } f(-x, y) = -f(x, y) \text{ (odd in } x\text{)}, \\ 2\iint_{R_{x \ge 0}} f(x, y)\,dA & \text{if } f(-x, y) = f(x, y) \text{ (even in } x\text{)}. \end{cases}$$ The exact same rule holds for $x$-axis symmetry ($y \mapsto -y$).

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 987, Ex. 11): Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{3} \int_{-\sqrt{9-x^2}}^{\sqrt{9-x^2}} (x + y)\,dy\,dx$.

The region $R$ is the centered disk $x^2 + y^2 \le 9$, which is symmetric about both the $y$-axis and the $x$-axis. Splitting by linearity gives $\iint_R x\,dA + \iint_R y\,dA$. Since $x$ is odd in $x$ and $y$ is odd in $y$, both integrals are $0$, so the result is $0$ with zero integration needed.

Why It Works: Domain additivity lets us split $R$ along an axis into $R_+ \cup R_-$ with opposite signs on the odd coordinate; substituting $u = -x$ flips the sign for odd functions so $\iint_{R_-} f\,dA = -\iint_{R_+} f\,dA$. For bounds, integrating the constant inequalities $m \le f(x,y) \le M$ by Theorem 14.1 Property 4 immediately produces $mA \le \iint_R f\,dA \le MA$.

Quick Check 3: Using symmetry and Theorem 14.1, what is the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} \int_{-\sqrt{4-x^2}}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}} (5 + x^3 y^2 - 2y)\,dy\,dx$?
(A) $0$ (B) $10\pi$ (C) $20\pi$ (D) $40\pi$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (C) $20\pi$. The domain is the disk $x^2 + y^2 \le 4$ of area $\pi(2)^2 = 4\pi$. Since $x^3 y^2$ is odd in $x$ and $-2y$ is odd in $y$, their integrals over the disk are $0$. Only the constant term remains: $\iint_R 5\,dA = 5\cdot\text{Area}(R) = 5(4\pi) = 20\pi$.
Core Concept • §4

4. Average Value of a Function Over a Region

Intuition: Imagine melting a sculpted ice block whose roof is $z = f(x, y)$ over a base mold $R$ of area $A$, and letting the water level out inside the exact same mold $R$ until the top is completely flat (Textbook p. 986). The volume $V = \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$ has not changed, so the flat water level $f_{\text{avg}}$ satisfies $f_{\text{avg}} \cdot \text{Area}(R) = V$. Dividing volume by base area gives the average value of $f$ over $R$.

Original solid volume $\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA$ Leveled block over same base $R$ Constant height $f_{\text{avg}}$

The average value $f_{\text{avg}}$ is the constant height of a flat-topped cylinder over $R$ whose volume equals $\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$ (Textbook p. 986).

Formula (Textbook p. 986 & Alhumaidy Notes): If $f$ is integrable over a plane region $R$ of area $A = \text{Area}(R) = \iint_R 1\,dA > 0$, then:

$$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{\text{Area}(R)} \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$$

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 988, Ex. 54 & Alhumaidy Notes): Find the average value of $f(x, y) = \frac{1}{x + y}$ over the triangle $R$ with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, and $(1, 1)$.

The base has length $1$ and height $1$, so $\text{Area}(R) = \frac{1}{2}(1)(1) = \frac{1}{2}$, and $R$ is $0 \le x \le 1$, $0 \le y \le x$. Therefore: $$\iint_R \frac{1}{x + y}\,dA = \int_0^1 \int_0^x \frac{1}{x + y}\,dy\,dx = \int_0^1 \Big[\ln(x + y)\Big]_{y=0}^{y=x}\,dx = \int_0^1 \big(\ln(2x) - \ln x\big)\,dx = \int_0^1 \ln 2\,dx = \ln 2.$$ Dividing by $A = \frac{1}{2}$ yields $f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\ln 2}{1/2} = 2\ln 2$.

Why It Works: On a discrete grid of $N$ equal subsquares of area $\Delta A = A/N$, the arithmetic mean of sample heights is $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i) = \frac{1}{N\Delta A}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i)\,\Delta A = \frac{1}{A}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i)\,\Delta A$, whose limit as $\|\Delta\| \to 0$ is $\frac{1}{A}\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$.

Quick Check 4 (KFUPM Final Term 233 Q15): What is the average value of $f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2$ over the square with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(0, 2)$, $(2, 0)$, and $(2, 2)$?
(A) $\dfrac{10}{3}$ (B) $\dfrac{8}{3}$ (C) $\dfrac{16}{3}$ (D) $\dfrac{32}{3}$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) $\dfrac{8}{3}$. Here $R = [0, 2] \times [0, 2]$ has $\text{Area}(R) = 4$. Next, $\int_0^2 \int_0^2 (x^2 + y^2)\,dy\,dx = \int_0^2 (2x^2 + \frac{8}{3})\,dx = \frac{16}{3} + \frac{16}{3} = \frac{32}{3}$. Dividing by $4$ gives $f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{32}{3} = \frac{8}{3}$.
Master Formulas

Section 14.2 Formula Reference & Edge Cases

Core Equations, Hypotheses & Edge Cases

  • Riemann Sum Definition (Textbook p. 980): For $f$ defined on a closed, bounded region $R$: $$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \lim_{\|\Delta\| \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i, y_i)\,\Delta A_i$$ Condition: Exists whenever $f$ is continuous on $R$ and $R$ is a finite union of nonoverlapping vertically/horizontally simple regions.
  • Volume Under & Between Surfaces (Textbook pp. 980, 985; Alhumaidy Notes): $$V = \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA \quad (f \ge 0 \text{ on } R), \qquad V = \iint_R \big(z_{\text{top}}(x, y) - z_{\text{bottom}}(x, y)\big)\,dA$$ Edge case: “First octant” adds $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, and $z \ge 0$ automatically — check that $z \ge 0$ across all of $R$.
  • Fubini’s Theorem (Textbook p. 982): For continuous $f$ on $R$: $$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy\,dx = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x, y)\,dx\,dy$$ Edge case: If $R$ is neither vertically nor horizontally simple (or a boundary changes formula midway), split $R = R_1 \cup R_2$ or switch to the order that keeps $R$ in one piece.
  • Bounds & Symmetry Shortcuts:
    • Constant & Bounds: $\iint_R k\,dA = k\cdot\text{Area}(R)$; if $m \le f(x, y) \le M$ on $R$, then $m\cdot\text{Area}(R) \le \iint_R f\,dA \le M\cdot\text{Area}(R)$.
    • Odd symmetry: $\iint_R f\,dA = 0$ ONLY if BOTH the region $R$ is symmetric across an axis AND $f$ changes sign across that same axis.
  • Average Value Over $R$ (Textbook p. 986): $$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{\text{Area}(R)} \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA, \qquad \text{Area}(R) = \iint_R 1\,dA > 0$$
Exam Traps

5 Classic Mistakes (WRONG vs. RIGHT)

Trap 1 — Blindly swapping limits when reversing integration order:

WrongRewriting $\int_0^1 \int_0^x f\,dy\,dx$ as $\int_0^x \int_0^1 f\,dx\,dy$ (leaves $x$ in the outer limit!).
RightSketch $R$ first: outer limits are always constants ($0 \le y \le 1$) and inner limits depend only on the outer variable ($y \le x \le 1$).

Trap 2 — Wrong shadow circle or upside-down subtraction $\Delta z$ between two surfaces:

WrongEquating $4 - x^2 - y^2 = 4 - 2x$ to get $x^2 + y^2 = 4$, or writing $(4 - 2x) - (4 - x^2 - y^2)$ without testing a point.
RightComplete the square: $x^2 - 2x + y^2 = 0 \implies (x - 1)^2 + y^2 = 1$, and test $(1, 0)$: $3 > 2$, so $\Delta z = (4 - x^2 - y^2) - (4 - 2x) = 2x - x^2 - y^2$.

Trap 3 — Forgetting $\dfrac{1}{\text{Area}(R)}$ (or using $b - a$) in Average Value:

WrongReporting $\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$ directly as $f_{\text{avg}}$, or dividing by $4 - 0 = 4$ instead of triangle area $\frac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4$.
RightAlways compute $A = \text{Area}(R)$ separately (e.g., $\frac{1}{2}bh$ for triangles, $a^2$ for squares) and divide: $f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{A}\iint_R f\,dA$.

Trap 4 — Claiming an odd integrand gives $0$ on a non-symmetric region:

WrongSaying $\iint_R x\,dA = 0$ on the first-quadrant sector $0 \le x \le \sqrt{25-y^2}$ because $x$ is an odd function.
RightOdd symmetry requires $R$ itself to be symmetric across the $y$-axis ($(-x, y) \in R$ whenever $(x, y) \in R$). In Quadrant I, $x \ge 0$ always, so $\iint_R x\,dA > 0$.

Trap 5 — Forgetting the “first octant” walls ($x = 0$, $y = 0$, $z = 0$):

WrongAssuming $z = 4 - y^2$, $y = x$, $y = 1$ needs another wall along $x$, or integrating past $z = 0$.
Right“First octant” supplies $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, $z \ge 0$, closing the base triangle with $x = 0$ to vertices $(0,0), (0,1), (1,1)$ (KFUPM Final 242 Q16).
Worked Examples

From Textbook Basics to KFUPM Final Level

Example 1 • Volume Under a Plane • Textbook p. 987 Ex. 23 & Alhumaidy Notes

Volume of a Tetrahedron in the First Octant

Use a double integral to find the volume of the solid in the first octant bounded by the plane $2x + 3y + 4z = 12$ and the coordinate planes.
Final Answer: $V = 12$.
1
Solve for $z$ and Find the Base Triangle $R$

Solving $2x + 3y + 4z = 12$ for $z$ gives the ceiling surface:

$$z = \frac{12 - 2x - 3y}{4}$$

Setting $z = 0$ locates the trace $2x + 3y = 12$ in the $xy$-plane. Together with $x \ge 0$ and $y \ge 0$, the base $R$ is the triangle with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(6, 0)$, and $(0, 4)$:

$$0 \le x \le 6, \qquad 0 \le y \le \frac{12 - 2x}{3}$$
2
Evaluate the Inner $y$-Integral
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \int_0^6 \int_0^{(12-2x)/3} \frac{12 - 2x - 3y}{4}\,dy\,dx \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\int_0^6 \left[(12 - 2x)y - \frac{3}{2}y^2\right]_{y=0}^{y=(12-2x)/3} dx \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\int_0^6 \left[\frac{(12 - 2x)^2}{3} - \frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{(12 - 2x)^2}{9}\right] dx \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\int_0^6 \frac{(12 - 2x)^2}{6}\,dx = \frac{1}{24}\int_0^6 4(6 - x)^2\,dx = \frac{1}{6}\int_0^6 (6 - x)^2\,dx \end{aligned}$$
3
Evaluate the Outer $x$-Integral
$$V = \frac{1}{6}\left[-\frac{(6 - x)^3}{3}\right]_0^6 = \frac{1}{18}\big(0 - (-6^3)\big) = \frac{216}{18} = 12$$
Verification: The solid is a right tetrahedron with intercepts $a = 6$, $b = 4$, $c = 3$, so its geometric volume is $V = \frac{1}{3}(\text{base area})(\text{height}) = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6 \cdot 4\right)(3) = 12$.
Example 2 • Reversing Order of Integration • Textbook p. 988 Ex. 50 & Alhumaidy Notes

Reversing Order to Eliminate a Non-Elementary Integral

Sketch the region of integration and evaluate the iterated integral: $$\int_0^2 \int_{x^2/2}^{2} \sqrt{y}\cos y\,dy\,dx$$
Final Answer: $\sqrt{2}\big(2\sin 2 + \cos 2 - 1\big)$.
1
Read the Region $R$ and Reverse the Order

The given limits describe $0 \le x \le 2$ and $\frac{x^2}{2} \le y \le 2$. The parabola $y = \frac{x^2}{2}$ meets the horizontal line $y = 2$ at $x^2 = 4 \implies x = 2$ (since $x \ge 0$), forming the region between $x = 0$, $y = 2$, and $x = \sqrt{2y}$.

Because $\int \sqrt{y}\cos y\,dy$ is not elementary, slice horizontally ($dx\,dy$):

$$0 \le y \le 2, \qquad 0 \le x \le \sqrt{2y}$$
2
Evaluate the Inner $x$-Integral
$$\int_0^2 \int_0^{\sqrt{2y}} \sqrt{y}\cos y\,dx\,dy = \int_0^2 \sqrt{y}\cos y\Big[x\Big]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{2y}}\,dy = \int_0^2 \sqrt{2}\,y\cos y\,dy$$
3
Integrate by Parts in $y$

Let $u = y$ and $dv = \cos y\,dy$, so $du = dy$ and $v = \sin y$:

$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{2}\int_0^2 y\cos y\,dy &= \sqrt{2}\left(\Big[y\sin y\Big]_0^2 - \int_0^2 \sin y\,dy\right) \\ &= \sqrt{2}\Big[y\sin y + \cos y\Big]_0^2 \\ &= \sqrt{2}\big((2\sin 2 + \cos 2) - (0 + \cos 0)\big) \\ &= \sqrt{2}\big(2\sin 2 + \cos 2 - 1\big) \end{aligned}$$
Verification: Differentiating the antiderivative gives $\frac{d}{dy}(y\sin y + \cos y) = \sin y + y\cos y - \sin y = y\cos y$, and checking the corner $y = 2$ gives $x \in [0, \sqrt{4}] = [0, 2]$, matching the original outer upper limit.
Example 3 • Volume Between Two Surfaces • KFUPM Final 251 Q16 & 243 Q5 / Textbook Ex. 35

Volume Bounded by a Paraboloid and a Tilted Plane

Set up an iterated double integral in the order $dy\,dx$ for the volume of the solid region bounded by the graphs of $z = 4 - x^2 - y^2$ and $z = 4 - 2x$.
Final Answer: $\displaystyle V = \int_0^2 \int_{-\sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2}}^{\sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2}} (2x - x^2 - y^2)\,dy\,dx$ (equivalently $\pm\sqrt{2x - x^2}$ on the inner limits).
1
Find the Projection $R$ by Equating $z$-Values
$$\begin{aligned} 4 - x^2 - y^2 &= 4 - 2x \\ x^2 - 2x + y^2 &= 0 \\ (x - 1)^2 + y^2 &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

The shadow $R$ in the $xy$-plane is the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(1, 0)$.

2
Determine $z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}}$

Test the center $(1, 0) \in R$: $z_{\text{paraboloid}}(1, 0) = 4 - 1 - 0 = 3$, whereas $z_{\text{plane}}(1, 0) = 4 - 2(1) = 2$. Since $3 > 2$, the paraboloid lies above the plane everywhere on $R$:

$$\Delta z = z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}} = (4 - x^2 - y^2) - (4 - 2x) = 2x - x^2 - y^2$$
3
Write the $dy\,dx$ Bounds Over the Disk $R$

From $(x - 1)^2 + y^2 \le 1$, $x$ runs across the diameter $[0, 2]$, and for each $x \in [0, 2]$, $y$ runs between $-\sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2}$ and $\sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2}$:

$$V = \int_0^2 \int_{-\sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2}}^{\sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2}} (2x - x^2 - y^2)\,dy\,dx$$
Verification: Rewrite $\Delta z = 2x - x^2 - y^2 = 1 - \big[(x - 1)^2 + y^2\big]$, which is strictly positive on the interior of the disk $(x-1)^2+y^2 < 1$ and $0$ on the boundary points $(0, 0)$, $(2, 0)$, and $(1, \pm 1)$.
Example 4 • Average Value & Order Reversal • KFUPM Final Term 253 Q16

Average Value of $4e^{y^2}$ Over a Triangle

Find the average value of $f(x, y) = 4e^{y^2}$ over the plane region $R$ bounded by the curves $y = 2x$, $y = 4$, and $x = 0$.
Final Answer: $f_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{e^{16} - 1}{4}$.
1
Sketch $R$ and Compute $\text{Area}(R)$

The three lines intersect pairwise at $(0, 0)$, $(0, 4)$, and $(2, 4)$, forming a right triangle with horizontal leg $2$ (along $y = 4$) and vertical leg $4$ (along $x = 0$):

$$\text{Area}(R) = \frac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4$$
2
Choose $dx\,dy$ to Avoid $\int e^{y^2}\,dy$

Since $e^{y^2}$ has no elementary $y$-antiderivative, slice horizontally: $0 \le y \le 4$ and $0 \le x \le \frac{y}{2}$.

$$\begin{aligned} f_{\text{avg}} &= \frac{1}{4}\int_0^4 \int_0^{y/2} 4e^{y^2}\,dx\,dy \\ &= \int_0^4 \left[x e^{y^2}\right]_{x=0}^{x=y/2} dy \\ &= \int_0^4 \frac{y}{2} e^{y^2}\,dy \end{aligned}$$
3
Evaluate by $u$-Substitution

Substitute $u = y^2$, so $du = 2y\,dy \implies \frac{y}{2}\,dy = \frac{1}{4}\,du$, with limits $u(0) = 0$ and $u(4) = 16$:

$$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{4}\int_0^{16} e^u\,du = \frac{1}{4}\Big[e^u\Big]_0^{16} = \frac{e^{16} - 1}{4}$$
Triangle $R$ bounded by $x=0$, $y=4$, $y=2x$ Horizontal slice $0 \le x \le y/2$ Triangle vertices & sweep direction

Drawn to true $1:1$ slope ($y = 2x$): slicing horizontally ($dx\,dy$) produces the factor $y/2$ needed for $u = y^2$ in the outer integral.

Verification: Differentiating gives $\frac{d}{dy}\left(\frac{1}{4}e^{y^2}\right) = \frac{y}{2}e^{y^2}$, and since $4 \le 4e^{y^2} \le 4e^{16}$ on $R$, the bounding property guarantees $4 \le f_{\text{avg}} \le 4e^{16}$, which holds for $\frac{e^{16}-1}{4}$.
Example 5 • Inverse Average Value • KFUPM Final Term 252 Q17

Finding an Unknown Square Side Length $a$ from $f_{\text{avg}}$

Let $f(x, y) = ax^2 + ay^2$, where $a > 0$ and $R = \{(x, y) : 0 \le x \le a,\; 0 \le y \le a\}$. If the average value of $f$ over $R$ is $18$, find $a$.
Final Answer: $a = 3$.
1
Set Up the Average Value Formula on $R = [0, a]^2$

The square $R$ has $\text{Area}(R) = a^2$, so:

$$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{a^2} \int_0^a \int_0^a (ax^2 + ay^2)\,dx\,dy$$
2
Evaluate the Double Integral in Terms of $a$
$$\int_0^a (ax^2 + ay^2)\,dx = \left[\frac{a x^3}{3} + a x y^2\right]_{x=0}^{x=a} = \frac{a^4}{3} + a^2 y^2$$ $$\int_0^a \left(\frac{a^4}{3} + a^2 y^2\right) dy = \left[\frac{a^4}{3}y + \frac{a^2 y^3}{3}\right]_{y=0}^{y=a} = \frac{a^5}{3} + \frac{a^5}{3} = \frac{2a^5}{3}$$
3
Solve $f_{\text{avg}} = 18$ for $a > 0$
$$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{a^2}\cdot\frac{2a^5}{3} = \frac{2}{3}a^3 = 18 \implies a^3 = 18\cdot\frac{3}{2} = 27 \implies a = 3$$
Verification: Plug $a = 3$ back in: $f(x, y) = 3x^2 + 3y^2$ on $[0, 3]\times[0, 3]$ ($\text{Area} = 9$). Then $\int_0^3\int_0^3 (3x^2 + 3y^2)\,dx\,dy = \int_0^3 (27 + 9y^2)\,dy = [27y + 3y^3]_0^3 = 81 + 81 = 162$, and $\frac{162}{9} = 18$.
One-Screen Summary

The 5 Things to Know for the Exam

  1. Volume between two surfaces is $\iint_R (z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}})\,dA$: Equate $z_1 = z_2$ (completing the square if needed) to find the shadow $R$, and test an interior point of $R$ to confirm which surface is on top.
  2. Always sketch $R$ before reversing the order of integration: Non-elementary inner integrals ($\int e^{-x^2}\,dx$, $\int e^{y^2}\,dy$, $\int \sin(y^2)\,dy$, $\int \sqrt{y}\cos y\,dy$) become elementary once you swap $dy\,dx \leftrightarrow dx\,dy$ correctly from the picture.
  3. Check odd/even symmetry and bounds before integrating: An odd integrand integrates to $0$ only if $R$ is symmetric across that axis; for bounds, $m \le f \le M$ gives $m\,\text{Area}(R) \le \iint_R f\,dA \le M\,\text{Area}(R)$.
  4. Average value always divides by $\text{Area}(R)$: Compute $f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{\text{Area}(R)}\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$ — never forget the $\frac{1}{A}$ factor, and compute triangle or square areas carefully.
  5. “First octant” supplies $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, and $z \ge 0$: Use $x = 0$ and $y = 0$ as automatic boundary walls of $R$, and verify $z \ge 0$ across all of $R$.
CONCEPT MASTERCLASS • SECTION 14.3

14.3 Change of Variables: Polar Coordinates

Larson & Edwards 7e (pp. 990–997) & Dr. Alhumaidy Notes — Polar Sectors & $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$, $r$-Simple vs. $\theta$-Simple Regions, Shifted Circles ($r = 2a\cos\theta$, $r = 2a\sin\theta$), Roses, Cardioids & Lines ($x = c$), Volume Between Surfaces, and Converting Cartesian Integrals to Polar.

Jump to section:
Lecture Video • 14.3 Polar Double Integrals
14.3 Double Integrals in Polar (28:05) — Covers polar area element $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$, radial ray bounds, volumes between surfaces, and shifted circles.
Watch on YouTube ↗
Jump to Timestamp:

What You Already Know

In Section 10.4, you learned how rectangular and polar coordinates convert via $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$, and $\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}$, and you found areas inside polar curves using $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta [g(\theta)]^2\,d\theta$ (Theorem 10.13). In Sections 14.1–14.2, you evaluated $\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$ by slicing $R$ into vertical or horizontal rectangles. When $R$ is a disk, annulus, cardioid, or sector — or when the integrand features $x^2 + y^2$ — Cartesian slices trap you in messy square roots like $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$. Switching to polar sectors turns curved circular boundaries into constant limits.

Core Concept • §1

1. Polar Sectors & Why $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$

Intuition: Instead of covering a circular region $R$ with little Cartesian squares of area $\Delta x\,\Delta y$, imagine laying down a spiderweb grid of concentric circles (radii $r_1, r_2, \dots$) and radial rays (angles $\theta_1, \theta_2, \dots$) as in Textbook pp. 990–991 (Figures 14.24–14.26). Each tiny wedge $R_i$ is a polar sector. Notice that two wedges with the exact same $\Delta r_i$ and $\Delta\theta_i$ do not have the same area: a wedge far from the origin has a much longer circular arc ($r_i \Delta\theta_i$) than one hugging the origin, so the area stretches proportionally to the radius $r_i$.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Larson & Edwards (p. 991) motivate the factor $r$ geometrically via polar sector area $\Delta A_i = r_i\Delta r_i\Delta\theta_i$ (deferring the formal Jacobian determinant $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = r$ to Section 14.8). Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes (p. 990) always write regions directly in explicit set-builder form $R = \{(r, \theta) : r_1 \le r \le r_2,\; \theta_1 \le \theta \le \theta_2\}$ beside the sketch and treat the extra $r$ in $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$ as the mandatory first check before integrating.
Polar sector $R_i$ in the $xy$-plane Corresponding rectangle $S_i$ in the $r\theta$-plane Average sample point $(r_i, \theta_i)$

A rectangle $S_i$ of area $\Delta r_i\Delta\theta_i$ in the $r\theta$-plane maps to a polar sector $R_i$ of area $\Delta A_i = r_i\Delta r_i\Delta\theta_i$, supplying the extra factor of $r$ (Textbook p. 991, Figures 14.26–14.27).

Formula (Theorem 14.3, Textbook p. 992): Let $R$ consist of all points $(x, y) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$ satisfying $0 \le g_1(\theta) \le r \le g_2(\theta)$ and $\alpha \le \theta \le \beta$ with $0 \le \beta - \alpha \le 2\pi$. If $g_1, g_2$ are continuous on $[\alpha, \beta]$ and $f$ is continuous on $R$, then:

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{g_1(\theta)}^{g_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta$$

Tiny Example (cf. Textbook p. 990 Ex. 1b & p. 995 Ex. 7): Evaluate $\iint_R (x^2 + y^2)\,dA$ where $R$ is the first-quadrant quarter-annulus $1 \le x^2 + y^2 \le 9,\; x \ge 0,\; y \ge 0$.

In polar coordinates, $R = \{(r, \theta) : 1 \le r \le 3,\; 0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}\}$ and $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$. Including $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$: $$\iint_R (x^2 + y^2)\,dA = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{1}^{3} r^2 \cdot r\,dr\,d\theta = \left(\int_{0}^{\pi/2} d\theta\right)\left(\int_{1}^{3} r^3\,dr\right) = \frac{\pi}{2} \left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_{1}^{3} = \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot \frac{81 - 1}{4} = 10\pi.$$

Why It Works (Textbook p. 997, Ex. 68): The exact area of the polar sector between radii $r_1, r_2$ and angles $\theta_1, \theta_2$ is the difference of two circular sectors: $$\Delta A_i = \frac{1}{2}r_2^2\Delta\theta_i - \frac{1}{2}r_1^2\Delta\theta_i = \frac{r_2 + r_1}{2}(r_2 - r_1)\Delta\theta_i = r_i\,\Delta r_i\,\Delta\theta_i,$$ where $r_i = \frac{r_1 + r_2}{2}$ is the average radius. Summing $f(r_i\cos\theta_i, r_i\sin\theta_i)\,r_i\,\Delta r_i\,\Delta\theta_i$ gives a Riemann sum over the $r\theta$-rectangle $S$ for the integrand $f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r$.

Quick Check 1: Let $R$ be the first-quadrant quarter-annulus $1 \le x^2 + y^2 \le 4,\; x \ge 0,\; y \ge 0$. Which iterated integral equals $\iint_R \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dA$?
(A) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\int_{1}^{2} r\,dr\,d\theta$ (B) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\int_{1}^{2} r^2\,dr\,d\theta$ (C) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\int_{1}^{4} r^2\,dr\,d\theta$ (D) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{1}^{2} r^2\,dr\,d\theta$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\int_{1}^{2} r^2\,dr\,d\theta$. Since $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ and $r \ge 0$, the integrand $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = r$, and $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$, giving $r \cdot r = r^2$. Also $1 \le r^2 \le 4 \implies 1 \le r \le 2$, and the first quadrant is $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$.
Core Concept • §2

2. $r$-Simple vs. $\theta$-Simple Regions via Radial Ray Sweep

Intuition: Just as rectangular regions split into vertically simple ($dy\,dx$) and horizontally simple ($dx\,dy$) types, polar regions split into $r$-simple and $\theta$-simple regions (Textbook p. 992, Figure 14.28). To set up an $r$-simple region, stand at the origin and fire a radial ray outward at an arbitrary angle $\theta$: the curve where the ray enters $R$ is $r_{\text{in}} = g_1(\theta)$ and the curve where it exits $R$ is $r_{\text{out}} = g_2(\theta)$, while you sweep the ray from $\theta = \alpha$ to $\theta = \beta$. If a radial ray would exit through two different curves (like a spiral plus a circle), switch to a $\theta$-simple slice: fix a radius $r \in [r_1, r_2]$ and sweep an arc counterclockwise from $\theta = h_1(r)$ to $\theta = h_2(r)$.

Radial ray sweep ($r$-simple) Circular arc sweep ($\theta$-simple) Spiral boundary $r = \frac{\pi}{3\theta}$ (Textbook p. 994 Ex. 5)

For $r$-simple regions, integrate $r$ first along a radial ray from $g_1(\theta)$ to $g_2(\theta)$; for $\theta$-simple regions like Example 5, integrate $\theta$ first along a circular arc from $h_1(r)$ to $h_2(r)$.

Formulas (Textbook pp. 992, 994):

  • $r$-Simple Order ($dr\,d\theta$): $\displaystyle\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{g_1(\theta)}^{g_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta$.
  • $\theta$-Simple Order ($d\theta\,dr$): $\displaystyle\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_{r_1}^{r_2} \int_{h_1(r)}^{h_2(r)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r\,d\theta\,dr$.

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 994, Example 5): Find the area of the region bounded above by the spiral $r = \frac{\pi}{3\theta}$ and below by the polar axis $\theta = 0$, between $r = 1$ and $r = 2$.

Solving $r = \frac{\pi}{3\theta}$ for $\theta$ gives $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3r}$, so $1 \le r \le 2$ and $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{3r}$. Integrating $\theta$ first makes the inner integral cancel $r$ immediately: $$A = \int_{1}^{2} \int_{0}^{\pi/(3r)} r\,d\theta\,dr = \int_{1}^{2} \Big[r\theta\Big]_{0}^{\pi/(3r)} dr = \int_{1}^{2} r\left(\frac{\pi}{3r}\right) dr = \int_{1}^{2} \frac{\pi}{3}\,dr = \left[\frac{\pi r}{3}\right]_{1}^{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}.$$

Why It Works: Look at Diagram 2(b) above: if you tried $dr\,d\theta$ on Example 5, a radial ray exits at $r = 2$ for $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{6}$ but exits at $r = \frac{\pi}{3\theta}$ for $\frac{\pi}{6} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{3}$, forcing two separate integrals! Circular arcs of constant $r \in [1, 2]$ enter cleanly at $\theta = 0$ and exit at $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3r}$ in a single integral.

Quick Check 2: Let $R$ be the first-quadrant region bounded by $r = 1$, $r = 3$, $\theta = 0$, and the spiral $r\theta = 1$. Which setup evaluates $\iint_R dA$ as a single iterated integral?
(A) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\int_{1}^{3} r\,dr\,d\theta$ (B) $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}\int_{0}^{1/r} r\,d\theta\,dr$ (C) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1/3}\int_{1}^{3} r\,dr\,d\theta$ (D) $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}\int_{0}^{1/r} d\theta\,dr$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}\int_{0}^{1/r} r\,d\theta\,dr$. Solving $r\theta = 1$ for $\theta$ gives $\theta = \frac{1}{r}$ as the exit angle on $1 \le r \le 3$, making $R$ $\theta$-simple. Don’t forget the $r$ in $dA = r\,d\theta\,dr$ (which eliminates choice D).
Core Concept • §3

3. Shifted Circles ($r = 2a\cos\theta$, $r = 2a\sin\theta$), Roses, Cardioids & Lines ($x = c$)

Intuition: Circles centered away from the origin — like $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = a^2$ or $x^2 + (y - a)^2 = a^2$ — still pass through $(0,0)$, so a radial ray starting at the origin enters at $r = 0$ and exits on the circle! The critical exam skill is matching the exact $\theta$-interval where $r(\theta) \ge 0$ so you trace the curve once without entering negative-$r$ territory. Similarly, straight lines like $x = c$ convert via $r\cos\theta = c \implies r = c\sec\theta$, while roses $r = a\cos(n\theta)$ or $r = a\sin(n\theta)$ require finding consecutive angles where $r = 0$ to isolate a single petal.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes (p. 995 Ex. 6 & Ex. 23, p. 996 Ex. 45 & Ex. 50) mark shifted circles and rose curves as “important” and require three exam habits: (1) complete the square on $y = \sqrt{2ax - x^2}$ to spot $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = a^2 \implies r = 2a\cos\theta$, (2) build a quick $(\theta, r)$ table to trace one petal and verify $r \ge 0$ rather than guessing limits, and (3) check whether an inner boundary vanishes before the outer boundary ends (e.g., in Textbook Ex. 50, inside $r = 1+\cos\theta$ and outside $r = 3\cos\theta$, the circle hits $r = 0$ at $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$ while the cardioid continues to $\theta = \pi$, splitting the integral at $\frac{\pi}{2}$).
Horizontal shifted circle $r = 2a\cos\theta$ Vertical shifted circle $r = 2a\sin\theta$ Single petal of rose $r = 2\sin 3\theta$

Shifted circles through the origin require half-plane $\theta$-bounds ($[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}]$ for $\cos\theta$ and $[0, \pi]$ for $\sin\theta$), while odd-petal roses trace one petal between consecutive roots of $r = 0$.

Key Equations & Standard Polar Bounds:

  • Horizontal shifted circle $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = a^2$ ($a > 0$): $r = 2a\cos\theta$ on $-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$ (upper half: $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$).
  • Vertical shifted circle $x^2 + (y - a)^2 = a^2$ ($a > 0$): $r = 2a\sin\theta$ on $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ (first-quadrant half: $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$).
  • Vertical / horizontal lines: $x = c \iff r = c\sec\theta$; $\; y = c \iff r = c\csc\theta$ (Textbook p. 996 Ex. 53).
  • Cardioids $r = a \pm a\cos\theta$ or $r = a \pm a\sin\theta$: $0 \le r \le r(\theta)$ with $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$ (always $r \ge 0$; e.g. $r = 1 + \cos\theta$ has area $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, Alhumaidy notes p. 996 Ex. 43).
  • Rose curves $r = a\cos(n\theta)$ or $r = a\sin(n\theta)$: $n$ petals if $n$ is odd; $2n$ petals if $n$ is even. Find one petal by solving $r(\theta) = 0$ for two adjacent roots where $r(\theta) \ge 0$.

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 994, Example 4): Find the total area enclosed by the 3-petal rose $r = 3\cos 3\theta$.

Solve $3\cos 3\theta = 0 \implies 3\theta = \pm\frac{\pi}{2} \implies \theta = \pm\frac{\pi}{6}$ for the right-hand petal (where $\cos 3\theta \ge 0$). By symmetry, total area is $3$ times one petal: $$A = 3\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}\int_{0}^{3\cos 3\theta} r\,dr\,d\theta = 3\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}\frac{9\cos^2 3\theta}{2}\,d\theta = \frac{27}{4}\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}(1 + \cos 6\theta)\,d\theta = \frac{27}{4}\left[\theta + \frac{1}{6}\sin 6\theta\right]_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} = \frac{9\pi}{4}.$$

Why It Works: Expanding $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = a^2$ gives $x^2 + y^2 = 2ax \implies r^2 = 2ar\cos\theta \implies r = 2a\cos\theta$. Because Theorem 14.3 enforces $r \ge 0$, we must restrict $\theta$ so $\cos\theta \ge 0$, which is $-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$ (not $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$, where $\cos\theta < 0$ in Quadrants II and III would re-trace the circle with negative $r$ and double the integral!).

Quick Check 3 (Textbook p. 995, Ex. 6 & Ex. 23): Which polar bounds describe the upper semicircular disk $0 \le x \le 2,\; 0 \le y \le \sqrt{2x - x^2}$?
(A) $0 \le \theta \le \pi,\; 0 \le r \le 2\cos\theta$ (B) $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2},\; 0 \le r \le 2\cos\theta$ (C) $-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2},\; 0 \le r \le 2\cos\theta$ (D) $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2},\; 0 \le r \le 2\sin\theta$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2},\; 0 \le r \le 2\cos\theta$. Squaring $y = \sqrt{2x - x^2}$ gives $(x - 1)^2 + y^2 = 1$ with $y \ge 0$, which is the upper half of $r = 2\cos\theta$ lying entirely in Quadrant I ($0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$).
Core Concept • §4

4. Converting Cartesian Integrals & Volumes to Polar Coordinates

Intuition: Two signals tell you to abandon rectangular $(x, y)$ coordinates and switch to polar: (1) circular boundaries such as $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$, $\sqrt{a^2 - y^2}$, or $\sqrt{2ax - x^2}$ in the limits of integration, and (2) radial expressions such as $x^2 + y^2$, $e^{-(x^2+y^2)}$, or $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ in the integrand (Textbook pp. 993, 995–996). Even better, a sum of two awkward Cartesian integrals over adjacent triangles and circular caps often glues together into a single circular sector in polar coordinates!

Triangle $R_1$ ($0 \le y \le x$) Circular wedge $R_2$ ($0 \le y \le \sqrt{8-x^2}$) Left half-disk ($x \le 0 \implies \frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi}{2}$)

Always sketch the Cartesian limits first: $R_1 \cup R_2$ collapses into a single $\frac{\pi}{4}$-sector, and $x \le 0$ selects $\theta \in [\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}]$ rather than $[0, \pi]$.

4-Step Conversion Protocol:

  1. Decode the limits: Sketch the bounding curves ($y = \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$ is the upper semicircle, $x = \sqrt{a^2 - y^2}$ is the right semicircle, $y = x$ is $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$ in Q1).
  2. Read polar bounds: Use a radial ray sweep to find $g_1(\theta) \le r \le g_2(\theta)$ and $\alpha \le \theta \le \beta$ (remember: $x \ge 0 \implies -\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$; $\; x \le 0 \implies \frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi}{2}$).
  3. Transform integrand & $dA$: Replace $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$, and $dx\,dy$ or $dy\,dx$ by $r\,dr\,d\theta$.
  4. For Volumes: If a solid lies between $z = z_{\text{bottom}}(x, y)$ and $z = z_{\text{top}}(x, y)$ over a base $R$, set $V = \iint_R (z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}})\,dA$ and convert both the height and $R$ to polar (Textbook p. 993 Ex. 3, p. 996 Ex. 33–38).

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 996, Ex. 38 & Alhumaidy Notes): Find the volume inside the upper hemisphere $z = \sqrt{16 - x^2 - y^2}$ (above $z = 0$) and outside the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 1$.

The hemisphere meets $z = 0$ at $x^2 + y^2 = 16$ ($r = 4$), so the base $R$ outside $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ ($r = 1$) is the annulus $1 \le r \le 4,\; 0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$, and height is $z = \sqrt{16 - r^2}$. Using $u = 16 - r^2$ ($du = -2r\,dr$): $$V = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{1}^{4} \sqrt{16 - r^2}\,r\,dr\,d\theta = 2\pi\left[-\frac{1}{3}(16 - r^2)^{3/2}\right]_{1}^{4} = \frac{2\pi}{3}\big(0 - (-15^{3/2})\big) = 10\sqrt{15}\pi.$$

Why It Works: Notice how the Jacobian factor $r$ in $r\,dr\,d\theta$ is the exact missing piece needed for $u$-substitution on $u = 16 - r^2$ (or $u = -r^2$ in Gaussian integrals like $e^{-(x^2+y^2)}$). Without that factor $r$, $\int \sqrt{16 - r^2}\,dr$ would require trig substitution!

Quick Check 4 (KFUPM Final Term 232 Q23): Which polar iterated integral equals $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{16 - x^2}} \cos(x^2 + y^2)\,dy\,dx$?
(A) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{-4}^{4} r\cos(r^2)\,dr\,d\theta$ (B) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{4} r\cos(r^2)\,dr\,d\theta$ (C) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{4} r\cos(r^2)\,dr\,d\theta$ (D) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{4} \cos(r^2)\,dr\,d\theta$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (C) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{4} r\cos(r^2)\,dr\,d\theta$. Since $0 \le y \le \sqrt{16 - x^2}$ and $-4 \le x \le 4$, $R$ is the upper half-disk of radius $4$ ($0 \le \theta \le \pi$, and radius is always $0 \le r \le 4$, never $-4$). Including $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$ rules out (D).
Master Formulas

Section 14.3 Formula Reference & Standard Regions

Core Laws, Bounds & Required Conditions

  • Coordinate Links & Area Element: $$x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad r^2 = x^2 + y^2, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}, \qquad dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$$
  • Theorem 14.3 ($r$-Simple Region): Requires $0 \le g_1(\theta) \le r \le g_2(\theta)$, $\alpha \le \theta \le \beta$, $0 \le \beta - \alpha \le 2\pi$, and continuous $f, g_1, g_2$: $$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{g_1(\theta)}^{g_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta$$
  • $\theta$-Simple Region: When $\theta$ is bounded cleanly as $0 \le h_1(r) \le \theta \le h_2(r)$ on $r_1 \le r \le r_2$: $$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_{r_1}^{r_2} \int_{h_1(r)}^{h_2(r)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r\,d\theta\,dr$$
  • Area & Volume via Polar Double Integrals: $$A = \iint_R 1\,dA = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{g_1(\theta)}^{g_2(\theta)} r\,dr\,d\theta \quad \Big(\text{if } g_1=0:\; \frac{1}{2}\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}[g_2(\theta)]^2\,d\theta\Big), \qquad V = \iint_R \big(z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}}\big)\,dA$$
  • Essential Half-Plane & Shifted-Circle $\theta$-Intervals ($r \ge 0$):
    • Disk $x^2+y^2 \le a^2$: $0 \le r \le a,\; 0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$.
    • Upper ($y \ge 0$): $0 \le \theta \le \pi$; $\;$ Right ($x \ge 0$): $-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$; $\;$ Left ($x \le 0$): $\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi}{2}$.
    • Shifted circle $(x-a)^2 + y^2 = a^2$: $r = 2a\cos\theta$, $-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$ (upper half: $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$).
    • Shifted circle $x^2 + (y-a)^2 = a^2$: $r = 2a\sin\theta$, $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ (right half: $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$).
    • Vertical line $x = c \implies r = c\sec\theta$; $\;$ Horizontal line $y = c \implies r = c\csc\theta$.
  • Trig Identities & Separability Shortcut: $$\cos^2(k\theta) = \frac{1 + \cos(2k\theta)}{2}, \qquad \sin^2(k\theta) = \frac{1 - \cos(2k\theta)}{2}$$ If all four limits are constants and the integrand factors as $h(r)k(\theta)$, then $\int_\alpha^\beta \int_a^b h(r)k(\theta)\,dr\,d\theta = \left(\int_a^b h(r)\,dr\right)\left(\int_\alpha^\beta k(\theta)\,d\theta\right)$.
Exam Traps

5 Classic Mistakes (WRONG vs. RIGHT)

Trap 1 — Dropping the polar factor $r$ in $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$:

WrongWriting $\iint_R \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dA = \int_\alpha^\beta \int_{g_1}^{g_2} r\,dr\,d\theta$.
Right$\sqrt{x^2+y^2} = r$ AND $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$, so the integrand is $r \cdot r = r^2$!

Trap 2 — Using $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$ on a shifted circle $r = 2a\cos\theta$ or $r = 2a\sin\theta$:

WrongSetting $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$ for the circle $r = 2\cos\theta$ or $r = 4\sin\theta$ (double-counts the area or makes $r < 0$).
RightKeep $r \ge 0$: use $-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$ for $r = 2a\cos\theta$, and $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ for $r = 2a\sin\theta$.

Trap 3 — Writing negative lower limits for $r$ or confusing a line $x = c$ with a circle:

WrongConverting $\int_{-4}^4 \int_0^{\sqrt{16-x^2}} dy\,dx$ to $-4 \le r \le 4$, or writing $x = 3 \implies r = 3$.
RightRadius is always $r \ge 0$ ($0 \le r \le 4$ for the half-disk), while a vertical line $x = c$ is $r\cos\theta = c \implies r = c\sec\theta$.

Trap 4 — Mixing up $\theta$-intervals for half-disks and $y = x$ sectors:

WrongUsing $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ for $x \le 0$ (that is $y \ge 0$!), or using $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{4}$ for $0 \le x \le y$.
Right$x \le 0$ is $\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi}{2}$; $x \ge 0$ is $-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$; $0 \le y \le x$ is $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{4}$; $0 \le x \le y$ is $\frac{\pi}{4} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$.

Trap 5 — Missing an angular split when the inner curve hits $r = 0$ (Textbook p. 996 Ex. 50 & Alhumaidy Notes):

WrongFor the region inside $r = 1+\cos\theta$ and outside $r = 3\cos\theta$, integrating $2\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi} \int_{3\cos\theta}^{1+\cos\theta} r\,dr\,d\theta$.
Right$3\cos\theta$ becomes $0$ at $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$! Split at $\frac{\pi}{2}$: $2\big[\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}\int_{3\cos\theta}^{1+\cos\theta} r\,dr\,d\theta + \int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\int_{0}^{1+\cos\theta} r\,dr\,d\theta\big]$.
Worked Examples

From Textbook Basics to KFUPM Final Level

Example 1 • Annular Region • Textbook p. 992 Example 2 & Alhumaidy Notes

Evaluating a Double Integral Over an Annulus

Let $R$ be the annular region lying between the two circles $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ and $x^2 + y^2 = 5$. Evaluate $$\iint_R (x^2 + y)\,dA.$$
Final Answer: $6\pi$.
1
Set Up Polar Bounds and Transform the Integrand

The circles $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ and $x^2 + y^2 = 5$ give $1 \le r \le \sqrt{5}$ around the full circle $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$. Substituting $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, and $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$:

$$\iint_R (x^2 + y)\,dA = \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{1}^{\sqrt{5}} (r^2\cos^2\theta + r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta = \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{1}^{\sqrt{5}} (r^3\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin\theta)\,dr\,d\theta$$
2
Evaluate the Inner $r$-Integral
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{1}^{\sqrt{5}} (r^3\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin\theta)\,dr &= \left[\frac{r^4}{4}\cos^2\theta + \frac{r^3}{3}\sin\theta\right]_{1}^{\sqrt{5}} \\ &= \left(\frac{25}{4} - \frac{1}{4}\right)\cos^2\theta + \left(\frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\right)\sin\theta \\ &= 6\cos^2\theta + \frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\sin\theta \end{aligned}$$
3
Use $\cos^2\theta = \frac{1+\cos 2\theta}{2}$ and Integrate with Respect to $\theta$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \left(3 + 3\cos 2\theta + \frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\sin\theta\right) d\theta &= \left[3\theta + \frac{3}{2}\sin 2\theta - \frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\cos\theta\right]_{0}^{2\pi} \\ &= \left(6\pi + 0 - \frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\right) - \left(0 + 0 - \frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\right) = 6\pi \end{aligned}$$
Verification: By symmetry of the annulus across the $x$-axis, $\iint_R y\,dA = 0$, and by rotational symmetry $\iint_R x^2\,dA = \iint_R y^2\,dA = \frac{1}{2}\iint_R (x^2 + y^2)\,dA = \frac{1}{2}(2\pi)\int_1^{\sqrt{5}} r^3\,dr = \pi\left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_1^{\sqrt{5}} = 6\pi$.
Example 2 • Shifted Circle Conversion • Textbook p. 995 Ex. 23 & Alhumaidy Notes

Converting $y = \sqrt{2x - x^2}$ to $r = 2\cos\theta$

Evaluate the iterated integral by converting to polar coordinates: $$\int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2x - x^2}} xy\,dy\,dx.$$
Final Answer: $\dfrac{2}{3}$.
1
Complete the Square to Identify the Shifted Circle

The bounds are $0 \le x \le 2$ and $0 \le y \le \sqrt{2x - x^2}$. Squaring $y = \sqrt{2x - x^2}$ (with $y \ge 0$) gives:

$$x^2 - 2x + y^2 = 0 \implies (x - 1)^2 + y^2 = 1$$

Thus $R$ is the upper half of the circle of radius $1$ centered at $(1, 0)$. In polar coordinates, $x^2 + y^2 = 2x \implies r^2 = 2r\cos\theta \implies r = 2\cos\theta$. Because $R$ lies entirely in Quadrant I ($x \ge 0,\; y \ge 0$), a radial ray sweeps $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$ with $0 \le r \le 2\cos\theta$.

2
Transform the Integral and Evaluate $r$ First
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2x - x^2}} xy\,dy\,dx &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{2\cos\theta} (r\cos\theta)(r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos\theta\sin\theta \left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{2\cos\theta} d\theta \\ &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos\theta\sin\theta \cdot \frac{16\cos^4\theta}{4}\,d\theta = 4\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos^5\theta\,\sin\theta\,d\theta \end{aligned}$$
3
Evaluate the $\theta$-Integral via $u = \cos\theta$

Let $u = \cos\theta$, so $du = -\sin\theta\,d\theta$. As $\theta: 0 \to \frac{\pi}{2}$, $u: 1 \to 0$:

$$4\int_{1}^{0} u^5(-du) = 4\int_{0}^{1} u^5\,du = 4\left[\frac{u^6}{6}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}$$
Upper semicircle $(x-1)^2 + y^2 = 1,\; y \ge 0$ Radial ray entering at $r=0$ and exiting at $r = 2\cos\theta$

Exact scale plot of Example 2: a radial ray at $\theta = \frac{\pi}{6}$ exits at $r = 2\cos\frac{\pi}{6} = \sqrt{3}$, i.e. $(1.5, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})$, and the upper half-disk spans $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$.

Verification: Integrate directly in Cartesian coordinates: $\int_0^2 x \left[\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^{\sqrt{2x-x^2}} dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^2 (2x^2 - x^3)\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{2}{3}(8) - 4\right] = \frac{2}{3}$.
Example 3 • Gaussian Half-Disk • KFUPM Final Term 253 Q17

Left Half-Disk Integral with $e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2}$

If $R = \{(x, y) : x^2 + y^2 \le 4,\; x \le 0\}$, evaluate $$\iint_R e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2}\,dA.$$
Final Answer: $(1 - e^{-2})\pi$.
1
Convert the Region $R$ to Polar Coordinates

The inequality $x^2 + y^2 \le 4$ gives radius $0 \le r \le 2$. Because $x \le 0$, the region lies in Quadrants II and III (left half-plane), where $\theta$ sweeps from the positive $y$-axis ($\frac{\pi}{2}$) to the negative $y$-axis ($\frac{3\pi}{2}$):

$$R = \left\{(r, \theta) : 0 \le r \le 2,\; \frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi}{2}\right\}$$
2
Rewrite the Integrand and Separate the Variables

Substitute $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ and $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$. Because the bounds are constants and the integrand depends only on $r$, factor the two 1D integrals:

$$\iint_R e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2}\,dA = \int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} \int_{0}^{2} r e^{-r^2/2}\,dr\,d\theta = \left(\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} d\theta\right)\left(\int_{0}^{2} r e^{-r^2/2}\,dr\right)$$
3
Evaluate Using $u = -r^2/2$

With $u = -\frac{r^2}{2}$, we have $du = -r\,dr$, and $r: 0 \to 2$ maps to $u: 0 \to -2$:

$$\int_{0}^{2} r e^{-r^2/2}\,dr = \left[-e^{-r^2/2}\right]_{0}^{2} = -e^{-2} - (-e^{0}) = 1 - e^{-2}$$

Multiplying by the angular length $\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} d\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{2} = \pi$ gives $(1 - e^{-2})\pi$.

Verification: The half-disk has area $\frac{1}{2}\pi(2^2) = 2\pi$, and on $R$ the integrand satisfies $e^{-2} \le e^{-r^2/2} \le 1$, so the integral must lie between $2\pi e^{-2} \approx 0.85$ and $2\pi \approx 6.28$; indeed $(1 - e^{-2})\pi \approx 2.72$.
Example 4 • Horizontal Cartesian Slices • KFUPM Final Term 251 Q18

Converting a $dx\,dy$ Sector Bounded by $x = y$

Evaluate the iterated integral: $$\int_{0}^{3/\sqrt{2}} \int_{y}^{\sqrt{9 - y^2}} \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dx\,dy.$$
Final Answer: $\dfrac{9\pi}{4}$.
1
Decode the $dx\,dy$ Bounds Into a Sketch

Here $y$ is the outer variable ($0 \le y \le \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$), and horizontal slices run from the left boundary $x = y$ (the ray $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$) to the right boundary $x = \sqrt{9 - y^2}$ (the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 9$ of radius $3$). Notice that $x = y$ meets $x^2 + y^2 = 9$ in Quadrant I at $2y^2 = 9 \implies y = x = \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$, and the bottom boundary is $y = 0$ ($\theta = 0$). Hence $R$ is the circular sector:

$$0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{4}, \qquad 0 \le r \le 3$$
2
Substitute $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = r$ and $dx\,dy = r\,dr\,d\theta$
$$\int_{0}^{3/\sqrt{2}} \int_{y}^{\sqrt{9 - y^2}} \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dx\,dy = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \int_{0}^{3} r \cdot r\,dr\,d\theta = \left(\int_{0}^{\pi/4} d\theta\right)\left(\int_{0}^{3} r^2\,dr\right)$$
3
Compute the Final Value
$$\frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \left[\frac{r^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{3} = \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \frac{27}{3} = \frac{9\pi}{4}$$
Verification: The sector has area $\frac{1}{8}\pi(3^2) = \frac{9\pi}{8}$. Since $0 \le r \le 3$, the average radial distance on a circular sector of radius $R$ is $\bar{r} = \frac{2}{3}R = 2$, and $\text{Area} \times \bar{r} = \frac{9\pi}{8} \cdot 2 = \frac{9\pi}{4}$.
Example 5 • Combining Two Integrals • KFUPM Final Term 243 Q6 & Textbook p. 995 Ex. 27

Gluing Two Cartesian Regions Into One Polar Sector

Write the sum of the two iterated integrals as a single polar iterated integral and evaluate: $$\int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{x} \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dy\,dx + \int_{2}^{2\sqrt{2}} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{8 - x^2}} \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dy\,dx.$$
Final Answer: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\int_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}} r^2\,dr\,d\theta = \dfrac{4\sqrt{2}\pi}{3}$.
1
Identify $R_1$ and $R_2$ and Check Their Seam at $x = 2$
  • $R_1$: $0 \le x \le 2$ and $0 \le y \le x$ (right triangle bounded by $y = 0$, $y = x$, and $x = 2$).
  • $R_2$: $2 \le x \le 2\sqrt{2}$ and $0 \le y \le \sqrt{8 - x^2}$ (region from $y = 0$ up to the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 8$ of radius $\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$).

As shown in Diagram 4(a), the ray $y = x$ intersects $x^2 + y^2 = 8$ at $2x^2 = 8 \implies (2, 2)$, right on the seam $x = 2$. Thus $R_1 \cup R_2$ is a single circular sector of radius $2\sqrt{2}$ between $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$.

2
Collapse Into One Polar Integral and Evaluate

With $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = r$ and $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$, both integrals merge into:

$$\begin{aligned} I &= \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \int_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}} r \cdot r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= \left(\int_{0}^{\pi/4} d\theta\right)\left(\int_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}} r^2\,dr\right) \\ &= \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \left[\frac{r^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \frac{(2\sqrt{2})^3}{3} = \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \frac{16\sqrt{2}}{3} = \frac{4\sqrt{2}\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Verification: Applying the sector formula $\frac{\pi}{12}R^3$ checked in Example 4 (where $R = 3$ gave $\frac{27\pi}{12} = \frac{9\pi}{4}$) with $R = 2\sqrt{2}$ gives $\frac{\pi}{12}(16\sqrt{2}) = \frac{4\sqrt{2}\pi}{3}$, and $(2\sqrt{2})^3 = 2^3(\sqrt{2})^3 = 8 \cdot 2\sqrt{2} = 16\sqrt{2}$.
One-Screen Summary

The 5 Things to Know for the Exam

  1. Never forget the polar factor $r$ in $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$: Every Cartesian area element $dx\,dy$ or $dy\,dx$ becomes $r\,dr\,d\theta$, and $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dA$ becomes $r^2\,dr\,d\theta$ (with $r \ge 0$).
  2. Sketch first and fire a radial ray from $(0,0)$: Entry curve is $g_1(\theta)$ and exit curve is $g_2(\theta)$; if a ray hits two different exit curves (or the boundary is $r\theta = c$), switch to $\theta$-simple order $r\,d\theta\,dr$.
  3. Lock in shifted-circle and half-plane $\theta$-bounds: $(x-a)^2+y^2=a^2 \iff r = 2a\cos\theta$ uses $-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$, while $x^2+(y-a)^2=a^2 \iff r = 2a\sin\theta$ uses $0 \le \theta \le \pi$; left half-disk ($x \le 0$) uses $\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi}{2}$.
  4. Handle roses and overlapping boundaries with a $(\theta, r)$ table: Solve $r(\theta) = 0$ for one petal of a rose, and split the $\theta$-integral whenever an inner boundary (like $r = 3\cos\theta$) reaches $r = 0$ before the outer curve ends.
  5. Separate constant-limit integrals and merge split Cartesian sectors: When limits are constant and the integrand factors as $h(r)k(\theta)$, evaluate $\left(\int h(r)\,dr\right)\left(\int k(\theta)\,d\theta\right)$, and check whether two adjacent Cartesian integrals (triangle + circular arc) combine into one clean sector.
CONCEPT MASTERCLASS • SECTION 14.6

14.6 Triple Integrals and Applications

Larson & Edwards 7e (pp. 1013–1023) & Dr. Alhumaidy Notes — Triple Iterated Integrals ($dV = dz\,dy\,dx$), All 6 Orders via 2D Coordinate-Plane Shadows ($xy$, $xz$, $yz$), Changing Order of Integration, Volume, Mass & Center of Mass.

Jump to section:
Lecture Video • 14.6 Triple Integrals
14.6 Triple Integrals (Rectangular) (16:17) — Covers rectangular triple integral bounds ($dz\,dy\,dx$) from roof/floor surfaces and 2D projections (first 5 minutes cover rectangular 14.6 before transitioning to cylindrical 11.7/14.7).
YouTube @ Starts at 00:18 ↗
Jump to Timestamp:

What You Already Know

In Section 14.2, you evaluated a double integral $\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA$ by slicing a flat 2D region $R$ either vertically ($dy\,dx$, Type I) or horizontally ($dx\,dy$, Type II), and reversing the order of integration when an antiderivative was non-elementary. In Section 14.3, you switched circular 2D regions to polar coordinates ($dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$). Section 14.6 lifts those exact slicing and reversal skills into 3D space: you first integrate along one coordinate between a floor and roof surface, then integrate over the resulting 2D shadow using your double-integral toolkit.

Core Concept • §1

1. Triple Iterated Integrals ($dV = dz\,dy\,dx$)

Intuition: Imagine packing a 3D solid region $Q$ tightly with tiny rectangular sugar cubes of dimensions $\Delta x_i$ by $\Delta y_i$ by $\Delta z_i$, each having volume $\Delta V_i = \Delta x_i \Delta y_i \Delta z_i$ (Textbook p. 1013, Figure 14.52). Multiply a function value $f(x_i, y_i, z_i)$ (such as density or temperature) at a sample point inside each cube by its tiny volume $\Delta V_i$, sum over every cube inside $Q$, and let the longest box diagonal $\|\Delta\| \to 0$. To compute this limit without summing millions of cubes, we stack cubes into vertical columns from a bottom surface $z = g_1(x, y)$ up to a top surface $z = g_2(x, y)$, then sweep those columns across the 2D floor shadow $R$ in the $xy$-plane (Textbook pp. 1014–1015, Theorem 14.4 & Figure 14.53).

Solid $Q$ between $z = g_1(x,y)$ and $z = g_2(x,y)$ Innermost $dz$ column over patch $dy\,dx$ 2D shadow $R$ on the $xy$-plane

For the order $dz\,dy\,dx$, first integrate vertically along $z$ from the floor surface $g_1(x,y)$ to the roof $g_2(x,y)$, then integrate over the 2D $xy$-shadow $R$ (cf. Textbook p. 1015, Figure 14.53).

Formula (Textbook pp. 1013–1014, Definition & Theorem 14.4): If $f$ is continuous on a $z$-simple solid region $Q$ described by $a \le x \le b$, $h_1(x) \le y \le h_2(x)$, and $g_1(x, y) \le z \le g_2(x, y)$, then:

$$\iiint_Q f(x, y, z)\,dV = \int_a^b \int_{h_1(x)}^{h_2(x)} \int_{g_1(x,y)}^{g_2(x,y)} f(x, y, z)\,dz\,dy\,dx$$

Triple integrals obey linearity and domain additivity over nonoverlapping subregions $Q = Q_1 \cup Q_2$:

$$\iiint_Q \big[c_1 f(x, y, z) \pm c_2 g(x, y, z)\big]\,dV = c_1 \iiint_Q f\,dV \pm c_2 \iiint_Q g\,dV, \qquad \iiint_{Q_1 \cup Q_2} f\,dV = \iiint_{Q_1} f\,dV + \iiint_{Q_2} f\,dV$$

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 1014, Example 1 & Alhumaidy Notes): Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_0^2 \int_0^x \int_0^{x+y} e^x(y + 2z)\,dz\,dy\,dx$.

Hold $x$ and $y$ constant for $dz$: $$\int_0^{x+y} e^x(y + 2z)\,dz = e^x\Big[yz + z^2\Big]_0^{x+y} = e^x\big(y(x+y) + (x+y)^2\big) = e^x(x^2 + 3xy + 2y^2)$$ Hold $x$ constant for $dy$: $$\int_0^x e^x(x^2 + 3xy + 2y^2)\,dy = e^x\left[x^2y + \frac{3}{2}xy^2 + \frac{2}{3}y^3\right]_0^x = e^x\left(1 + \frac{3}{2} + \frac{2}{3}\right)x^3 = \frac{19}{6}x^3 e^x$$ Finally integrate with respect to $x$ (using integration by parts three times, as written in Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes pp. 1014–1015): $$\frac{19}{6}\int_0^2 x^3 e^x\,dx = \frac{19}{6}\Big[e^x(x^3 - 3x^2 + 6x - 6)\Big]_0^2 = \frac{19}{6}\big(e^2(8 - 12 + 12 - 6) - (-6)\big) = \frac{19}{6}(2e^2 + 6) = 19\left(\frac{e^2}{3} + 1\right)$$

Why It Works: Holding the outer two variables constant during the innermost integral turns a 3D problem into a single-variable Calculus I integral along a line segment piercing $Q$. Once integrated out, that variable disappears completely, leaving a standard 2D double integral over the shadow $R$.

Quick Check 1 (Textbook p. 1021 Ex. 10 & Alhumaidy Notes): What is the exact value of $\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/2} \int_0^{y/2} \int_0^{1/y} \sin y\,dz\,dx\,dy$?
(A) $1$ (B) $\dfrac{1}{2}$ (C) $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (D) $\dfrac{1}{4}$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) $\dfrac{1}{2}$. Inner $z$-integral: $\int_0^{1/y} \sin y\,dz = \frac{\sin y}{y}$. Middle $x$-integral: $\int_0^{y/2} \frac{\sin y}{y}\,dx = \frac{\sin y}{y}\cdot\frac{y}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\sin y$. Outer $y$-integral: $\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin y\,dy = \frac{1}{2}\big[-\cos y\big]_0^{\pi/2} = \frac{1}{2}(0 + 1) = \frac{1}{2}$.
Core Concept • §2

2. All 6 Orders of Integration via 2D Coordinate-Plane Shadows

Intuition: Because there are $3! = 6$ ways to order $dx$, $dy$, and $dz$ ($dz\,dy\,dx$, $dz\,dx\,dy$, $dy\,dx\,dz$, $dy\,dz\,dx$, $dx\,dy\,dz$, $dx\,dz\,dy$), every simple solid $Q$ admits six equivalent iterated integrals (Textbook pp. 1013, 1015). Regardless of which order you pick, the strategy is always the same two-step Spear & Shadow method: first fire a ray parallel to the innermost axis to read its entry and exit surfaces; then squash $Q$ onto the coordinate plane of the outer two variables to read their 2D bounds.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): In his handwritten notes on Textbook p. 1015 (Example 2) and p. 1021 (Exercises 14 & 18), Dr. Alhumaidy emphasizes two practical exam habits: (1) always draw the 2D shadow separately with a directional slice arrow matching the middle differential, and (2) when $Q$ is bounded by two surfaces $z = g_1(x, y)$ and $z = g_2(x, y)$ that meet above the $xy$-plane, find the shadow boundary by setting $g_1(x, y) = g_2(x, y)$ (“equate them”) rather than setting $z = 0$.
$xy$-shadow ($z=0$) for $dz\,dy\,dx$ / $dz\,dx\,dy$ $xz$-shadow ($y=0$) for $dy\,dz\,dx$ / $dy\,dx\,dz$ $yz$-shadow ($x=0$) for $dx\,dy\,dz$ / $dx\,dz\,dy$

Exact 2D shadows for the tetrahedron $x + 2y + 3z \le 6$ ($x,y,z \ge 0$): each innermost differential determines which variable you solve for first, while the outer two differentials govern the slice direction in the corresponding 2D shadow.

All 6 Orders Recipe (Illustrated for $Q: x + 2y + 3z \le 6,\; x,y,z \ge 0$):

  • $dz$ innermost ($xy$-shadow $x + 2y \le 6$): $$\int_0^6 \int_0^{(6-x)/2} \int_0^{(6-x-2y)/3} f\,dz\,dy\,dx \quad = \quad \int_0^3 \int_0^{6-2y} \int_0^{(6-x-2y)/3} f\,dz\,dx\,dy$$
  • $dy$ innermost ($xz$-shadow $x + 3z \le 6$): $$\int_0^6 \int_0^{(6-x)/3} \int_0^{(6-x-3z)/2} f\,dy\,dz\,dx \quad = \quad \int_0^2 \int_0^{6-3z} \int_0^{(6-x-3z)/2} f\,dy\,dx\,dz$$
  • $dx$ innermost ($yz$-shadow $2y + 3z \le 6$): $$\int_0^3 \int_0^{(6-2y)/3} \int_0^{6-2y-3z} f\,dx\,dz\,dy \quad = \quad \int_0^2 \int_0^{(6-3z)/2} \int_0^{6-2y-3z} f\,dx\,dy\,dz$$

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 1017, Example 4a & 4c):

(a) Find the volume bounds for the first-octant solid below $z = 1 - y^2$ and between the vertical planes $x + y = 1$ and $x + y = 3$. Since $0 \le z \le 1 - y^2$ and the $xy$-shadow is a parallelogram with two horizontal sides $y = 0$ and $y = 1$, slice horizontally ($dx$ before $dy$): $1 - y \le x \le 3 - y$, $0 \le y \le 1$, giving $V = \int_0^1 \int_{1-y}^{3-y} \int_0^{1-y^2} dz\,dx\,dy$.

(c) Set up $V$ for the solid bounded below by $z = x^2 + y^2$ and above by $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 6$. Here $x^2 + y^2 \le z \le \sqrt{6 - x^2 - y^2}$. To find the $xy$-shadow, equate $z$: substitute $x^2 + y^2 = z$ into $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 6$ to get $z + z^2 = 6 \implies (z+3)(z-2) = 0$. Since $z \ge 0$, they intersect at $z = 2$, so the shadow is the disk $x^2 + y^2 \le 2$: $$V = \int_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}} \int_{-\sqrt{2-x^2}}^{\sqrt{2-x^2}} \int_{x^2+y^2}^{\sqrt{6-x^2-y^2}} dz\,dy\,dx$$ (This exact setup appeared on KFUPM Final Term 232 Q24.)

Why It Works: For a solid lying between two surfaces $z = g_1(x,y)$ and $z = g_2(x,y)$ that do not rest on $z = 0$, the solid exists only where the floor lies beneath the roof: $g_1(x,y) \le g_2(x,y)$. Thus the outer rim of its vertical shadow onto the $xy$-plane is always the intersection curve $g_1(x,y) = g_2(x,y)$.

Quick Check 2 (Textbook p. 1021 Ex. 18 & Alhumaidy Notes): For the solid bounded above by the cylinder $z = 4 - x^2$ and below by the paraboloid $z = x^2 + 3y^2$, what curve bounds its projection onto the $xy$-plane?
(A) $x^2 + 3y^2 = 4$ (B) $2x^2 + 3y^2 = 4$ (C) $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ (D) $x = \pm 2$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) $2x^2 + 3y^2 = 4$. Following Dr. Alhumaidy’s rule (“equate them”), set the lower and upper $z$-surfaces equal: $x^2 + 3y^2 = 4 - x^2 \implies 2x^2 + 3y^2 = 4$, an ellipse in the $xy$-plane.
Core Concept • §3

3. Changing the Order of Triple Integration

Intuition: Sometimes a triple integral is handed to you in an order that traps an impossible inner integral (such as $\int \sin(y^2)\,dy$ or $\int e^{y^2}\,dy$), or forces piecewise splitting across corners. Because the value of a triple integral over $Q$ is independent of the order of integration (Textbook p. 1016), you can rescue the integral by translating the given limits back into 3D inequalities, sketching $Q$ (“draw!” as Dr. Alhumaidy writes on p. 1021 Ex. 25), and slicing in a better order.

Vertical prism $1 \le z \le 3$ over $0 \le x \le y \le \sqrt{\pi/2}$ Original slice ($dy$ inner) hits $\int \sin(y^2)\,dy$ Reversed slice ($0 \le x \le y$) creates $y\sin(y^2)$

In Textbook p. 1016 Example 3, $1 \le z \le 3$ decouples from $(x,y)$, so switching $dz\,dy\,dx \to dz\,dx\,dy$ only flips the $xy$-triangle from $x \le y \le \sqrt{\pi/2}$ to $0 \le x \le y$.

4-Step Order-Reversal Method:

  1. Extract inequalities: Write down the lower and upper bounds for all three variables directly from the limits.
  2. Identify & sketch $Q$: Rewrite curved/plane inequalities (e.g., $z \le \frac{12-3x-6y}{4} \iff 3x+6y+4z \le 12$) to see the 3D surfaces bounding $Q$.
  3. Pick the new innermost bounds: Solve the bounding surface inequalities for the new innermost variable.
  4. Re-project onto the new outer plane: Squash $Q$ onto the plane of the remaining two variables and read Type I or Type II bounds.

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 1016, Example 3): Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_0^{\sqrt{\pi/2}} \int_x^{\sqrt{\pi/2}} \int_1^3 \sin(y^2)\,dz\,dy\,dx$.

Evaluating $dz$ gives $2\int_0^{\sqrt{\pi/2}} \int_x^{\sqrt{\pi/2}} \sin(y^2)\,dy\,dx$, where $\sin(y^2)$ has no elementary antiderivative in $y$. From the limits $0 \le x \le \sqrt{\pi/2}$ and $x \le y \le \sqrt{\pi/2}$ (with $1 \le z \le 3$), the $xy$-region is the upper triangle $0 \le x \le y \le \sqrt{\pi/2}$. Changing to $dz\,dx\,dy$ puts $0 \le x \le y$ and $0 \le y \le \sqrt{\pi/2}$: $$\int_0^{\sqrt{\pi/2}} \int_0^y \int_1^3 \sin(y^2)\,dz\,dx\,dy = 2\int_0^{\sqrt{\pi/2}} \left(\int_0^y \sin(y^2)\,dx\right) dy = 2\int_0^{\sqrt{\pi/2}} y\sin(y^2)\,dy = \Big[-\cos(y^2)\Big]_0^{\sqrt{\pi/2}} = 0 - (-1) = 1$$ (The exact same triangle reversal solves KFUPM Final 251 Q1 and Final 252 Q6.)

Why It Works: Reversing $dy\,dx \to dx\,dy$ while keeping $dz$ innermost multiplies $\sin(y^2)$ by the horizontal strip width $\int_0^y dx = y$, supplying the exact factor $y\,dy = \frac{1}{2}du$ needed for the substitution $u = y^2$.

Quick Check 3 (Textbook p. 1021 Ex. 25, starred in Alhumaidy Notes): Which integral equals $\displaystyle \int_0^1 \int_{-1}^0 \int_0^{y^2} dz\,dy\,dx$ in the order $dy\,dz\,dx$?
(A) $\displaystyle \int_0^1 \int_0^1 \int_{\sqrt{z}}^1 dy\,dz\,dx$ (B) $\displaystyle \int_0^1 \int_0^1 \int_{-1}^{-\sqrt{z}} dy\,dz\,dx$ (C) $\displaystyle \int_0^1 \int_0^1 \int_{-\sqrt{z}}^0 dy\,dz\,dx$ (D) $\displaystyle \int_0^1 \int_{-1}^0 \int_0^{\sqrt{z}} dy\,dz\,dx$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) $\displaystyle \int_0^1 \int_0^1 \int_{-1}^{-\sqrt{z}} dy\,dz\,dx$. From the limits, $0 \le x \le 1$ is independent, while in the $yz$-plane $-1 \le y \le 0$ and $0 \le z \le y^2$. Because $y$ is negative, $z \le y^2$ and $y \ge -1$ yield $-1 \le y \le -\sqrt{z}$ for $0 \le z \le 1$. (Volume check: $\int_0^1 \int_0^1 \int_{-1}^{-\sqrt{z}} dy\,dz\,dx = \int_0^1 (1 - \sqrt{z})\,dz = \frac{1}{3}$, matching $\int_0^1 \int_{-1}^0 y^2\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{3}$.)
Core Concept • §4

4. Applications: Volume, Mass, Center of Mass & Average Value

Intuition: Setting the integrand $f(x,y,z) = 1$ adds up pure box volumes $\Delta V_i$ to yield the Volume of $Q$. If $Q$ is made of a material whose mass density $\rho(x, y, z)$ varies from point to point (for example, heavier away from the origin), integrating $\rho(x,y,z)\,dV$ adds up tiny box masses $dm = \rho\,dV$ to get total Mass $m$. Weighting each tiny mass by its signed distance to the three coordinate planes gives the first moments $M_{yz}, M_{xz}, M_{xy}$, and dividing by $m$ yields the 3D balance point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z})$ — the Center of Mass (Textbook pp. 1018–1019).

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Dr. Alhumaidy’s annotated PDF marks “Center of Mass and Moments of Inertia” (Textbook pp. 1018–1020, Examples 5–6) with a skip mark ($\alpha$/$\times$) while circling Volume exercises (pp. 1021–1022) and Average Value (p. 1023, Exercises 63 & 66). We include Mass & Center of Mass plus Average Value here for complete 14.6 mastery, while omitting Moments of Inertia.
Unit cube $Q = [0,1]^3$ Uniform centroid $\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)$ Variable-density center of mass $\left(\frac{7}{12}, \frac{7}{12}, \frac{7}{12}\right)$

In Textbook p. 1019 Example 5, because $\rho(x,y,z) = k(x^2+y^2+z^2)$ is heaviest near $(1,1,1)$, the center of mass shifts outward past the geometric center $\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\right)$ to $\left(\frac{7}{12},\frac{7}{12},\frac{7}{12}\right)$.

Formulas (Textbook pp. 1013, 1018, 1023):

  • Volume: $V = \iiint_Q dV$
  • Mass ($m$) & First Moments: $$m = \iiint_Q \rho(x, y, z)\,dV, \qquad M_{yz} = \iiint_Q x\rho(x, y, z)\,dV, \qquad M_{xz} = \iiint_Q y\rho(x, y, z)\,dV, \qquad M_{xy} = \iiint_Q z\rho(x, y, z)\,dV$$
  • Center of Mass $(\bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z})$: $$\bar{x} = \frac{M_{yz}}{m}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{M_{xz}}{m}, \qquad \bar{z} = \frac{M_{xy}}{m}$$
  • Average Value of $f$ over $Q$: $$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{V} \iiint_Q f(x, y, z)\,dV$$

Tiny Example (Textbook p. 1019, Example 5): Find the center of mass of the unit cube $0 \le x, y, z \le 1$ with density $\rho(x,y,z) = k(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)$ ($k > 0$).

First compute the mass: $$m = k\int_0^1 \int_0^1 \int_0^1 (x^2 + y^2 + z^2)\,dz\,dy\,dx = k\int_0^1 \int_0^1 \left(x^2 + y^2 + \frac{1}{3}\right)\,dy\,dx = k\int_0^1 \left(x^2 + \frac{2}{3}\right)\,dx = k\left[\frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{2x}{3}\right]_0^1 = k$$ Now compute $M_{yz}$, factoring $x$ out of the inner $dy\,dz$ integrals: $$M_{yz} = k\int_0^1 x\left[\int_0^1 \int_0^1 (x^2 + y^2 + z^2)\,dz\,dy\right] dx = k\int_0^1 x\left(x^2 + \frac{2}{3}\right) dx = k\left[\frac{x^4}{4} + \frac{x^2}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{7k}{12}$$ Hence $\bar{x} = \frac{M_{yz}}{m} = \frac{7k/12}{k} = \frac{7}{12}$, and by symmetry of $x, y, z$ in both $Q$ and $\rho$, $(\bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z}) = \left(\frac{7}{12}, \frac{7}{12}, \frac{7}{12}\right)$.

Why It Works: Why does $\bar{x}$ use $M_{yz}$ (and not $M_{xy}$)? Because the $yz$-plane has equation $x = 0$, so the signed perpendicular lever arm of a point $(x, y, z)$ from the $yz$-plane is $x$. Likewise, $y$ is the distance from the $xz$-plane ($y=0$), and $z$ is the distance from the $xy$-plane ($z=0$). Also, when $\rho$ is constant, $\rho$ cancels out of $\frac{M_{yz}}{m}$ and the center of mass becomes the purely geometric centroid.

Quick Check 4 (Textbook p. 1023 Ex. 63 & Ex. 66, circled in Alhumaidy Notes): Find the average value of $f(x, y, z) = z^2 + 4$ over the unit cube in the first octant bounded by the coordinate planes and $x = 1$, $y = 1$, $z = 1$.
(A) $\dfrac{1}{3}$ (B) $\dfrac{13}{3}$ (C) $4$ (D) $\dfrac{14}{3}$
Check Answer & Reason
Answer: (B) $\dfrac{13}{3}$. The unit cube has volume $V = 1^3 = 1$. Then $f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{1}\int_0^1 \int_0^1 \int_0^1 (z^2 + 4)\,dz\,dy\,dx = \int_0^1 (z^2 + 4)\,dz = \left[\frac{z^3}{3} + 4z\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3} + 4 = \frac{13}{3}$. (Compare with Ex. 66: for $f(x,y,z)=x+y$ over the symmetric sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2 \le 3$, odd symmetry immediately gives $f_{\text{avg}} = 0$.)
Master Formulas

Section 14.6 Formula Reference & Edge Cases
